articles.title: Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Election Looms: Is This Old Wine in a New Bottle?
articles.full_text:
The shape of the Kazakh legislature may have changed, but the politics of Kazakhstan have not necessarily been transformed.
On August 23, Kazakh citizens will head to the polls to cast votes for the country’s new legislative body, the 145-seat unicameral Kurultai. 
The Kurultai – not to be confused with the National Kurultai, a government-civil society consultative body formed by Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in 2022 after the Qandy Qantar events and dissolved this summer – was established with the passage of the constitutional referendum in June. Named for a traditional political and military council convened by Mongol and Turkic peoples, Kazakhstan’s new Kurultai replaces its previous bicameral parliament.
The shape of the Kazakh legislature may have changed, but the politics of Kazakhstan have not necessarily been transformed. 
There are seven political parties contesting the elections following the June 12 merger of Amanat – the ruling party, formerly known as Nur-Otan – with the upstart Adilet. While opposition political parties have struggled in vain for years to obtain registration, the newly formed Adilet raced from nonexistence to registration in record time. Importantly, Aibek Dadebay, very recently the head of the presidential administration, is the party’s head. 
In the previous 98-seat lower house, the Majilis, Amanat secured 62 seats in the 2023 election. No other party came close: Auyl held eight seats, Respublica and Aq Jol held six each, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan (QHP) held five, and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (JSDP) held four seats.
Adilet is expected to dominate in the upcoming polls. Is this just old wine in a new bottle? Perhaps. The genuine test is what comes after the election: how the new legislature operates and whether there is not just room for genuine debate but actual debate in that room. If the legislature serves, as its predecessors have, as merely a rubber stamp on the president’s projects then indeed Kazakhs will be sipping an ancient vintage once again. 
According to Kazakhstan’s Central Election Commission (CEC), as of July 23, it had registered 545 candidates for the 145 seats. The 2023 election operated under a mixed system for the first time since 2004, in which 69 seats were allocated via party-lists and 29 by constituency. This year, all 145 seats in the Kurultai will be elected via proportional representation according to party lists. This heightens the importance of parties, but absent new parties this may just serve as a non-electoral limit on who can participate in governance. 
Mere days ahead of the election, major Kazakh media outlets – those not directly under state control – are carrying very little that can be construed as election coverage. Vlast and Tengrinews, for example, both reported on the free public transport being offered on August 23 in Almaty and Astana. There are also reports on the number of election observers registered. There are few (if any) reports on the platforms being put forward by the individual parties. 
Reports in state media slot each party into a natural constituency without offering much detail about how those parties approach universal problems. Auyl – the Kazakh word for “village” – “focused on agricultural development and rural communities,” according to the Astana Times. Aq Jol and Respublica “continued to compete for entrepreneurs and economically liberal voters, with both parties emphasizing business development and market-oriented reforms.” 
Kazakhstan’s non-state media also carried reports on a statement issued by a constellation of human rights organizations calling on the Kazakh government to cease its persecution of and pressure on journalists and media outlets ahead of the election. The signatures included the International Foundation for the Protection of Freedom of Speech “Adil soz,” the Kazakhstan International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law, the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Araminta, Civil Right Defenders, Crude Accountability, Freedom For Eurasia, and the International Partnership for Human Rights.
In the August 14 statement, the human rights organizations directed attention to the arrest in July of political commentator Azamat Omarov; the travel bans against Lukpan Akhmedyarov and Dinara Yegeubayeva, who are both under investigation for separate incidents rife with irregularities ; and the sentencing of journalist Aleksandra Alyokhova to three years following her conviction under a data privacy law.
“These cases form part of a broader, longer-term pattern of increasing pressure on independent media and journalists in Kazakhstan, including the use of politically motivated charges, online restrictions on access to information, and other forms of harassment and intimidation against those who criticize the authorities,” the statement argued. 
Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and Information, Aida Balayeva, appeared to respond to the statement with a lengthy Facebook post on August 17, though she primarily focused on “information being disseminated about the alleged mass blocking of a number of media accounts, activists, and bloggers.”
Balayeva reiterated that Kazakhs have an “indisputable right to carry out journalistic and blogging activities.”
“The Ministry of Culture and Information does not block social media user accounts, including those of media outlets and journalists. Such actions are a clear tool for discrediting the state and its institutions and are aimed at hindering the ministry’s efforts to ensure freedom of speech,” Balayeva wrote.
Balayeva stressed that the right to speech is paired with a responsibility to accuracy.
“At the same time, it is crucial to clearly distinguish between illegal materials and legitimate expression of opinion, professional journalistic activity, and public debate. The fight against illegal content should not become a basis for unjustified restrictions on freedom of speech,” Balayeva wrote.

articles.title: Are Allies’ Military AI Systems Interoperable?
articles.full_text:
The U.S., South Korea, and Japan are pursuing different AI-driven combat systems. That will lead to different recommendations on the same battlefield.
Soldiers assigned to the 304th Expeditionary Signal Battalion-Enhanced install and inspect communications equipment in support of Ulchi Freedom Shield at CP Tango in South Korea, Aug. 11, 2026.
How can allies using different AI systems on the same battlefield trust one another? While current discussions about military artificial intelligence (AI) focus on simply fielding these systems, allied militaries soon have to address this exact question. 
In 2025, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and Scale AI tested seven major foundation models across 400 diplomatic and security scenarios. Despite being presented with identical international crises, the recommendations from the seven models diverged significantly. Some were uniquely hawkish, and every model exhibited some degree of national bias. This demonstrates that AI is by no means a homogenous tool.
Now these fractured algorithms are being integrated into many militaries on earth. We may be living through one of the final eras where an AI-equipped military might face an opponent operating without it. Before long, most global alliances will be thoroughly armed with AI – but each will be operating with a radically different version. Consequently, the real question is no longer who possesses AI, but rather, whether allies can trust different AI systems on the same battlefield. 
Nations are already scrambling to secure interoperability between their chosen AI frameworks and those of their allies. The United States is rapidly strengthening AI-driven interoperability within its Indo-Pacific alliances. For instance, during the September 2025 Freedom Edge trilateral exercise between the United States, South Korea, and Japan, the nations demonstrated real-time data exchange by linking their respective simulation systems using AI tools.
The scope of these discussions is vast, ranging from real-time sensor integration and instant target identification to improving allied AI literacy. On the surface, this sounds like traditional alliance cooperation rhetoric, but beneath it lies cutting-edge military technology poised to reshape how coalition warfare operates.
The problem lies in what comes next. If every ally adopted Palantir’s Maven Smart System, for instance, integration would be relatively straightforward. However, with the rise of “AI sovereignty,” nations are parting ways on which AI-driven combat systems to adopt.
Japan has adopted a calculated two-track strategy, with summer 2026 being the watershed. Before June, under the Japan-U.S. alliance framework, Tokyo actively leveraged existing U.S. systems when necessary, while fostering domestic companies like SoftBank and Sakura Internet as the pillars of its sovereign AI infrastructure. Microsoft and Open AI’s recent investment signings with the aforesaid Japanese tech giants, while on a commercial basis, definitely seemed to be a signal that Tokyo would not rule out U.S. AI capabilities taking root in Japanese soil. 
Perhaps the adoptions of Palantir-based solutions by Japanese firms, namely Fujitsu, was a harbinger of a bold change. As of mid-August, Japan is considering Palantir’s Maven Smart System as well as Anduril’s Lattice. The government, according to Nikkei, “envisions bringing in multiple AI systems” for the best operational decision-making, while using different systems for specific, tailored applications. This is best interpreted as a dual strategy that leverages U.S. technology while cultivating domestic industry to safeguard sensitive Self-Defense Force information and intelligence.
South Korea, by contrast, leans toward building systems based on independent technology rather than adopting U.S. platforms. With the government declaring 2026 as the year of the Defense AI Transformation, Naver recently launched a dedicated defense AI organization, entering the military market with its own foundation models and sovereign AI capabilities. Private-sector competition is heating up as SK Telecom and Hanwha Systems join the fray. 
Meanwhile, the Philippines has yet to chart a clear direction. Lacking large domestic AI enterprises, it may quickly and boldly adopt foreign platforms like Palantir in the future.
Like any multilateral security initiative, this plan to connect disparate AI systems into a single, integrated decision-making structure demands a core requirement that must be met. Deploying and operating AI is one thing; accurately understanding the capabilities and limitations of an ally’s system is an entirely different matter.
The critical link is highly likely to be a concept that, despite its immense importance, has flown under the radar: the Risk Management Framework (RMF). Verification is required at two distinct levels. Traditional RMFs handle the security accreditation and interoperability standards of the middleware connecting different platforms. However, the newer, less familiar dimension of AI model trustworthiness is handled by an AI-specific layer within that framework – specifically, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI RMF. Though largely invisible, the AI RMF could become the true unsung hero that binds U.S.-made systems and indigenous allied AIs into a single, integrated network.
The aforementioned CSIS and Scale AI experiment highlights the issue: If models diverge this drastically in judgment, binding different AI systems into a single operation without verification is dangerous. Yet, forcing the same system onto everyone is impossible, as the reality of AI sovereignty is already pulling nations in different directions. Only one answer remains: permit the use of different models, but verify their trustworthiness using the same yardstick. That yardstick is the AI RMF developed by NIST specifically for AI.
Take a computer vision AI used for target identification as an example. In automated target recognition, the reliability of distinguishing threats from civilians, or friends from foes, is decisive in actual combat. A model that achieves 99 percent accuracy on a sunny training range cannot be trusted on the battlefield based on that metric alone.
The AI RMF fills this exact void by providing a framework that makes trustworthiness measurable and comparable. It quantitatively reveals how resilient the model is when an adversary attempts to deceive it via camouflage or spoofing. It shows how much identification accuracy degrades in environments outside its training data, such as fog or nighttime, and how reliability fluctuates under poor sensor data quality. This falls into the realm of inherent AI model trustworthiness – a domain untouched by standard cybersecurity checks. 
The AI RMF does not simply give a system a passing stamp; it translates a system’s strengths and breaking points into actionable data that a commander can read. When this measured data accumulates, a Korean system and a U.S. system, for instance – even with entirely different internal architectures – can have their trustworthiness compared on the exact same basis.
This measurement matters not just for technical accuracy, but because it directly relates to whether humans can maintain genuine control over AI. When discussing autonomous systems, the phrase “human-in-the-loop” is frequently used. However, there is a vast difference between a human sitting in that loop as a mere formality and a human who substantively controls the system by understanding the rationale behind its judgments. Giving approval without knowing where an AI is reliable and where it is likely to make mistakes is not meaningful control; it is rubber-stamping. The trustworthiness data generated by the AI RMF provides commanders with that necessary understanding of the system’s strengths and weaknesses. A truly trustworthy AI is, ultimately, an AI that a human can control based on evidence.
The necessity of the AI RMF extends even further. In the current rush to field AI on the battlefield, it is easy to miss the fact that you cannot have maximum performance and maximum security simultaneously. Making an AI highly resilient against enemy deception often blunts its speed and accuracy; conversely, pushing solely for raw performance leaves the system vulnerable to manipulation. Gaining ground on one side requires sacrificing some on the other. The AI RMF quantifies this trade-off by showing exactly where each system stands between security and performance. 
At this juncture, the AI RMF transcends individual system verification to become the common language of the alliance. When integrating different AI systems into a single operation, nations can look at the measured data and mutually agree on where to set the baseline of trust for a specific coalition mission. Determining that balance remains a human responsibility, but without these measurements, such an agreement becomes a baseless compromise.
In its June 5, 2026, National Security Presidential Memorandum (NSPM-11), the United States established its national security AI policy on four pillars: adoption, adaptation, assurance, and accountability. Among these, “assurance” dictates that deployed AI must be reliable, robust, steerable, and controllable. The memorandum explicitly directed the creation of standardized Test, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation methodologies for national security AI. The message is clear: even the fastest-moving nation has begun treating verification not as a bureaucratic formality that delays adoption, but as a prerequisite that enables integration.
This shift went beyond policy declarations. In early June 2026, DARPA, NSF, and NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) jointly launched AI Forge, a national program devoted to building the assurance foundations of national-security AI: interpretability, control, adversarial robustness, and credible, verifiable benchmarks. If NSPM-11 set “verified AI” as a policy principle, AI Forge began building the technical foundation to actually make that verification possible – and the fact that NIST anchors one of its pillars reinforces the argument that AI RMF can become the common yardstick binding allies together.
If allies cannot trust each other’s AI, they cannot fight together. This is the low-profile yet essential foundation that the AI RMF provides. Allies will succeed only when each nation can verify the other’s AI against a common standard of trust – and continue to verify those systems as they evolve.

articles.title: Beyond Kashmir: South Asia’s Other Territorial Disputes
articles.full_text:
These disputes all involve India and the Himalayas – but in these three cases, the other claimant isn’t Pakistan.
An Indian Army outpost in remote Arunachal Pradesh.
You probably have heard of Kashmir – the Muslim-majority region that India and Pakistan have fought three different wars over. But the Kashmir Valley isn’t the only contentious border dispute in South Asia, even if it’s the only one most people have heard of.
Today, we’re going to talk about three other territorial disputes in the region – the sort of flashpoints that stay below the headlines until it’s too late. In fact, two of these disputes have seen shots fired in recent years – and it could happen again. 
Stay tuned, because we’re ranking them in order: from the least likely to spark an actual shooting war to the highest risk of conflict.

articles.title: Kim Min-seok Wins Democratic Party Chair in Ranked-Choice Runoff
articles.full_text:
The former prime minister defeated incumbent chair Jung Chung-rae 54.1 percent to 45.9 percent in the party’s chairmanship election.
Kim Min-seok speaks at a joint campaign event event for Democratic Party chair and Supreme Council candidates in Naju Sports Park, Naju, South Korea, Aug. 15, 2026.
Former Prime Minister Kim Min-seok was elected as the leader of the ruling Democratic Party (DP), closing out a six-week race that exposed deep rifts between rival camps aligned with South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and outgoing party chair Jung Chung-rae.
Kim, a four-term lawmaker, won 54.08 percent of the final vote announced at the party’s national convention in Daejeon, defeating Jung, who took 45.92 percent. Kim fell short of a first-round majority under the combined count of member, delegate, and opinion-poll votes, triggering the party’s ranked-choice runoff for the first time in its history. Under that process, second-choice votes from backers of third-place finisher Rep. Song Young-gil were redistributed between Kim and Jung, producing Kim’s final voting margin. 
The new DP leader will oversee candidate nominations for the general elections in April 2028. More than that, the race was widely seen as a test of how firmly Lee has consolidated control over the DP since assuming presidency in 2025. The contest has widely been described as a proxy fight between the pro-Lee camp and a harder-line faction associated with Jung, who has at times pushed back against the presidential office on the pace of judicial overhaul and other issues. Kim’s campaign speech in July framed the race as a referendum on whether the party would fully back Lee’s agenda,
Kim’s strongest results came in Gwangju and the Jeolla provinces and the greater Seoul area after Lee announced an 800 trillion won ($564 billion) semiconductor investment package for the Gwangju region. Overall, however, Lee’s approval rating slipped to 44 percent in recent days, the lowest since he took office, according to local media reports.
This was the DP’s first party chair race under the new one-member, one-vote system. Dues-paying members and delegates account for 70 percent of the weight, and a national opinion survey makes up the remaining 30 percent. 
The public opinion poll was conducted over two days by two polling firms among a combined 4,000 respondents reached by automated phone survey, with participation limited to Democratic Party supporters and independents to screen out backers of the conservative opposition.
Because no rule guarantees a majority winner, the party adopted ranked-choice voting: if no candidate clears 50 percent on first-preference ballots, the last-place finisher is eliminated and votes are reallocated by second choice.
The voting took place in waves, with results announced region by region. Voting opened August 1 in Chungcheong, where Kim narrowly outpolled Jung, 45.05 percent to 44.61 percent, with Song a distant third at 10.34 percent. Jung answered the next day in Busan, Ulsan, and South Gyeongsang Province, beating Kim 46.65 percent to 43.85 percent. Kim then won Jeju and Incheon on August 8 with 47.75 percent to Jung’s 42.08 percent, and a fourth round spanning Gangwon Province, Daegu and North Gyeongsang Province followed on August 9, with Kim ahead 48.54 percent to 44.40 percent and the cumulative gap narrowing to 1.48 points.
The race turned decisively in Kim’s favor on August 15 in Gwangju and the Jeolla provinces, the party’s largest single bloc of members at roughly a third of the total. Kim won 57.54 percent there to Jung’s 32.65 percent, pushing his cumulative share past 50 percent for the first time. The final regional round, in Seoul and Gyeonggi Province on August 16, went to Kim by a far tighter margin, 46.66 percent to 46.28 percent, pulling his majority back below 50 percent and leaving him with an overall cumulative lead of 49.91 percent to 41.51 percent heading into August 17 and the party’s national convention.
Alongside the chair, on August 17 the DP seated five Supreme Council members from an eight-candidate field. Voters picked two of the eight names and the five candidates with the highest combined vote share won seats, with the top finisher becoming senior Supreme Council member. Five of the eight candidates were aligned with the pro-Lee camp – Rep. Park Sun-won, Rep. Kim Yong, Rep. Seo Mi-hwa, Rep. Kim Young-ho, and Rep. Im Mi-ae – while three were aligned with Jung’s camp – Rep. Choi Min-hee, Rep. Han Min-soo, and Rep. Lee Sung-yoon.
Late on August 16, two lower-ranked pro-Lee candidates, Im Mi-ae and Kim Young-ho, dropped out of the race and threw their support behind Kim Yong, in an effort to consolidate pro-Lee votes and prevent Jung’s camp from taking three of the five seats.
The final results confirmed a split verdict. Choi finished first by vote share and will serve as senior Supreme Council member, followed in order by Park Sun-won, Seo Mi-hwa, Lee Sung-yoon and Han Min-soo. Three of the five seats went to lawmakers aligned with Jung while only two went to pro-Lee lawmakers. Kim Yong, the candidate whom Im and Kim Young-ho withdrew to support, fell short of a seat despite their last-minute endorsement.
The outcome leaves incoming DP chair Kim Min-seok with a Supreme Council in which lawmakers aligned with his defeated rival hold a majority of the elected seats. The divide is likely to complicate Kim’s efforts to consolidate the party behind President Lee heading into the 2028 general elections.
Kim, the new leader of the DP, belongs to South Korea’s so-called 86 generation, student activists who led the pro-democracy movement of the 1980s and later entered mainstream politics. As Seoul National University’s student council president, he was recruited into politics in 1990 by the late President Kim Dae-jung and joined the merger of Kim’s party with the New Democratic Alliance Party, earning him the nickname “first son of democratic unification.” Elected to the National Assembly in 1996 at age 32, he was the youngest lawmaker of his time and won a second term in 2000.
His rise stalled in October 2002, when he left the party during a dispute over unifying the presidential candidacies of Roh Moo-hyun and Chung Mong-joon, a decision that resurfaced repeatedly as a line of attack from Jung during the campaign. Kim lost his Assembly seat in 2004 and spent several years outside elected politics, including periods of study in the United States and China. He returned to the party’s leadership as a Supreme Council member in 2008 but was later barred from running for office for five years over a political funding case. He founded a small breakaway party in 2014 before it merged back into the DP in 2016 under then-chair Choo Mi-ae.
Kim won back a National Assembly seat in 2020 and secured a fourth term in 2024. His alignment with Lee Jae-myung deepened during the 2022 presidential race, when he headed strategy for Lee’s campaign. Kim went on to serve as the DP’s policy chief and, from 2024, as senior Supreme Council member under Lee’s own chairmanship. After Lee’s election as president following the impeachment of Yoon Suk-yeol, Kim was named the first prime minister of the Lee administration in mid-2025, a post in which he oversaw the APEC summit in Gyeongju and met with U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance in Washington before stepping down at the end of June 2026 to run for party chair. He is now regarded within the DP as a potential future presidential contender.

The final regional round, in Seoul and Gyeonggi Province on August 16, went to Kim by a far tighter margin, 46.66 percent to 46.28 percent, pulling his majority back below 50 percent and leaving him with an overall cumulative lead of 49.91 percent to 41.51 percent heading into August 17 and the party’s national convention.
Alongside the chair, on August 17 the DP seated five Supreme Council members from an eight-candidate field. Voters picked two of the eight names and the five candidates with the highest combined vote share won seats, with the top finisher becoming senior Supreme Council member. Five of the eight candidates were aligned with the pro-Lee camp – Rep. Park Sun-won, Rep. Kim Yong, Rep. Seo Mi-hwa, Rep. Kim Young-ho, and Rep. Im Mi-ae – while three were aligned with Jung’s camp – Rep. Choi Min-hee, Rep. Han Min-soo, and Rep. Lee Sung-yoon.
Late on August 16, two lower-ranked pro-Lee candidates, Im Mi-ae and Kim Young-ho, dropped out of the race and threw their support behind Kim Yong, in an effort to consolidate pro-Lee votes and prevent Jung’s camp from taking three of the five seats.
The final results confirmed a split verdict. Choi finished first by vote share and will serve as senior Supreme Council member, followed in order by Park Sun-won, Seo Mi-hwa, Lee Sung-yoon and Han Min-soo. Three of the five seats went to lawmakers aligned with Jung while only two went to pro-Lee lawmakers. Kim Yong, the candidate whom Im and Kim Young-ho withdrew to support, fell short of a seat despite their last-minute endorsement.
articles.summary: The former prime minister defeated incumbent chair Jung Chung-rae 54.1 percent to 45.9 percent in the party’s chairmanship election.

articles.title: India’s Collapsing Roads and Highways Dent Modi Government’s Image
articles.full_text:
It has built dozens of expressways and highways at enormous cost. But these have not survived the stress test of even the season’s first rains.
A screenshot of a video by The Lallantop showing the condition of the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway, four months after its inauguration by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
A video clip of India’s Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari is going viral these days in which he claims that a Dubai prince once asked Prime Minister Narendra Modi to “export” him to Dubai for six months.
According to the minister, the Dubai royal was so impressed by India’s rapidly expanding road infrastructure that he wanted Gadkari to replicate it in Dubai.
Both Modi and Gadkari, while highlighting the success stories of India’s highway construction, claimed that India is now using space technology in road construction and that by 2024, India’s roads could be comparable with roads in the United States.
It is a good story. It is also an irresistible one for a politician who has spent more than a decade selling India’s highway construction as one of the great success stories of the Narendra Modi era.
There is no doubt that India has developed a vast network of roads connecting major cities and reducing travel time.
However, these much-hyped expressways have not withstood the stress test of even the season’s first rains.
India’s social media has been flooded with video clips showing how these expressways have developed potholes and cracks during the first spell of the monsoon this year.
The biggest story was the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway, inaugurated by Modi on April 14 at a reported cost of about $1.258 billion, which developed large potholes and cracks just three months after its opening.
The biggest ridicule was directed at the government when the Kanpur-Lucknow Expressway, barely weeks after its inauguration, caved in. To avoid embarrassment, the government launched repair works, but the sight of industrial electric fans lined up along a freshly built expressway to dry out waterlogged soil further dented the government’s claims.
Then came the Pune-Mumbai Expressway Missing Link, built at a cost of about $701.93 million. Pothole-like patches appeared on the newly inaugurated stretch after the first waves of monsoon rain.
The Delhi-Mumbai Expressway has not escaped the monsoon stress test. A contractor’s contract was terminated by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) after repeated failures to meet contractual requirements.
Indians are accustomed to navigating potholes during the monsoon season, but deep craters on high-speed expressways could be life-threatening for drivers.
The newly built expressways and national highways across and between major Indian cities have developed cracks, potholes or structural failures soon after opening, raising serious questions about construction quality, supervision and accountability.
Gadkari, who was already facing people’s outrage over adding ethanol to petrol, has disappeared from public life. One doesn’t know whether he attended the recently concluded monsoon session of Parliament.
The NHAI has initiated proceedings to declare PNC Infratech, the developer of the Lucknow-Kanpur Expressway, a non-performing contractor after glaring lapses emerged in the construction quality of the newly inaugurated corridor.
The Times of India, in its editorial titled “Pothole Nation,” said this characterizes recurring highway craters as systemic failures stemming from corruption and poor construction oversight.
In an article titled “It’s roads to ruin as Indians count cost of Modi, the motorway PM,” The London Times argued that Modi’s infrastructure boom is impressive in scale but increasingly marred by poor construction and failures. The newly built roads, bridges, airport roofs and underpasses have repeatedly developed serious problems.
It pointed to around 170 bridge collapses between 2021 and 2025, causing about 200 deaths, along with several airport and road failures.
The potholes and cracks will be repaired in due course, but no action can repair the damage to the Modi government’s image as a champion of a corruption-free India.

articles.title: The Dilemma Facing Malaysia’s Democratic Action Party
articles.full_text:
Until 2022, the DAP had spent six decades in opposition – but gaining a foothold in government has been a mixed blessing.
Members of the Democratic Action Party (DAP) attend a special party conference at the Putrajaya International Convention Center in Putrajaya, Malaysia, Aug. 16, 2026.
Poor electoral performances in the Sabah, Johor, and Negeri Sembilan Malaysian state elections overshadowed the Democratic Action Party (DAP)’s national congress on August 16.
The extraordinary congress was called in the wake of the disappointing return in Negeri Sembilan on August 1, which analysts said was due to the government’s perceived mishandling of corruption cases and concerns over its commitment to promised reforms.
The DAP leadership subsequently decided to convene a special national congress, at which it would table a motion on whether the party should remain a part of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government.
Although the party voted in favor of remaining a part of the government, the meeting highlighted the DAP’s predicament over what cost the party is paying for finally tasting the fruits of power.
The 60-year-old party, once seen as the most vocal opponent of the old Malay establishment, today has to remain “silent” on the shortcomings of Anwar’s government, including alleged corruption charges.
It was this silence which reverberated loudly during the congress as most delegates were concerned about the party losing appeal among its core voters,  urban and semi-urban ethnic Chinese communities. Results of the three state elections reflected this, as the party lost seats which it had held for three consecutive terms.
Sangeet Kaur Deo, the daughter of the late prominent Malaysian lawyer and DAP stalwart Karpal Singh, raised the issue of the party’s silence on many issues concerning corruption. Sangeet said voters had questioned DAP’s silence on too many issues, like the discharge not amounting to an acquittal granted to Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on 47 corruption charges in September 2023.
“So stay in government and speak up while we are there. And if we must become opposition again, at least we have laid the basis and regained credibility,” she said.
She urged the DAP’s Central Executive Committee to “seriously reassess” its relationship with Anwar, whom she accused of dividing coalition partners, pitting them against one another and strengthening the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) – the primary component of the Barisan Nasional coalition, which is part of Anwar’s unity government – at the DAP’s expense.
Sangeet also challenged the party’s reason for joining the government: that its ministers would help implement the reforms long promised to voters.
“If we were, we would have done it already,” she said, adding that DAP should use the next 18 months in government to speak up on issues of concern and rebuild its credibility.
Although there was no official reaction to Sangeet’s appeal, it found resonance in DAP National Chairman Gobind Singh Deo’s statement, in which he called on Anwar to immediately accelerate several long-awaited institutional reforms, including the separation of the attorney general and public prosecutor roles and the creation of a two-term limit for the prime minister.
Gobind said the decision by DAP delegates at the party’s National Congress to remain in the federal government sent a clear message that the party’s core reform agenda must now be implemented without further delay.
“While the party has voted to remain in the Federal Government, urgent and concrete steps must now be taken to implement our core agenda, specifically institutional and economic reforms,” he said.
He urged Prime Minister Anwar to set clear and firm timelines for the implementation of foundational institutional reforms.
The challenge that the DAP has faced since entering government in late 2022 is how to manage the transition from vocal opposition party to silent coalition partner.
Winning power is the ultimate goal of any political outfit; that was the aim of DAP as well. Now, it is in power but is in danger of losing the appeal that brought it to this point.
How DAP manages to achieve these dual objectives will be the biggest challenge of its six-decade existence, as it moves from being Malaysia’s most successful opposition party to becoming a part, and possibly a permanent one, of the country’s political establishment.

articles.title: Extreme Heat Is Hurting South Asia’s Economies. Here’s How Much.
articles.full_text:
Multiple reports highlight alarming loss of wages and work hours due to extreme heat.
Exposure to extreme heat is costing the South Asian workforce a significant chunk of their pay every year, a series of recently published reports show. The single largest economic cost of heat comes from labor productivity losses, but there are other factors as well. A report from the World Bank predicted that South Asia’s regional GDP could be reduced by nearly 7 percent by 2050 if no adaptation measures are taken.
A recent report from Bangladesh, which is based on interviews with 175 households engaged in informal work such as construction, rickshaw pulling, and garment manufacturing, found that outdoor workers lost about 8.5 percent of their annual income, as they lost roughly 24 working days a year. Indoor workers lost 14 working days and 4.5 percent of their annual income. For both groups, illness caused by heat and reduced productivity are the largest causes of workdays lost.
The report, titled “No escaping the heat: Health and economic impacts of heat stress on informal workers in urban Bangladesh,” estimates the nation is losing about 0.9 percent of its GDP due to workday losses. That figure further increases if the cost of kidney-related ailments due to frequent dehydration is taken into account. Workers reported low mood, mistakes at work, anxiety, and irritability, as well as difficulty sleeping.
The London-headquartered International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) conducted the study jointly with the Dhaka-based Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP). The report comes close on the heels of two other publications that point to similar findings for the South Asian region.
A July 2026 report by IIED said India’s nationwide cost of heat-related kidney problems, combined with employees’ reduced ability to work during heatwaves, is estimated to be $78 billion in lost wages – equivalent to 1.99 percent of India’s GDP in 2024. Based on a survey conducted on 538 informal worker households in three Indian cities, Ajmer, Delhi, and Agra, the IIED study found a picture very similar to that of Bangladesh.
Those in outdoor industries like construction, road laying and brickmaking lost about 24 days of work annually due to heat, costing them the equivalent of $151 — nearly a tenth of their annual earnings. Indoor workers engaged in food packaging, garment manufacturing, and stonemasonry lost roughly 15 days — the equivalent of $89.
The overall loss of work hours translates to a massive scale of lost employment opportunities. Regarding South Asia, a World Bank report, titled “A Livable Future: Tackling Extreme Heat for Jobs and Growth in South Asia’s Cities,” published at the end of July, said that extreme heat “already subtracts the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs a year across the region.”
The report examines how urban heat threatens the job market in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. It estimates that, on average, rising temperatures will lower labor productivity in South Asia by 11 percent below the baseline by 2050. This is the largest estimated loss for any emerging market and developing economy region.
As another 2026 report on South and Southeast Asian cities, titled “Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder,” points out, even in a Himalayan city like Nepal’s Kathmandu, 85 percent of respondents reported wage losses and increased healthcare expenses due to extreme heat. In Delhi, they found workers risk being sent home without pay when the heat slows output and targets are missed.
Sri Lanka is not immune from heat stress either. A 2025 study reported that the island nation lost a total of $10.87 billion in 2023 due to reduced work hours.
According to Ritu Bharadwaj, IIED’s director of climate resilience, finance, and loss and damage, for these workers, heat exposure doesn’t end when their shift ends. “They leave a hot worksite for a home with a tin roof, one fan, and frequent power cuts, giving no chance to recover,” she said.
Across South Asia, many informal workers in megacities and other urban settlements live in slums. Their homes are built of substandard materials, have tin or asbestos roofs and little ventilation, and are usually cramped for space.
The World Bank report says that while heat reduces productivity in existing work, it also discourages investments required for new jobs. Health burden and cooling have their own cost. For example, 90 percent of New Delhi’s street vendors reduced working hours due to heat in summer 2025, while 72 percent lost their stock of perishable food items to heat damage.
Power outages add to the crisis. When temperatures exceed 40 degrees Celsius, power outages in India increase by 20-50 percent, with the duration rising proportionally. Without action, cooling could account for 45 percent of India’s peak electricity load by 2050, up from 10 percent in 2016. This will not only put pressure on industrialization, but also leave workers with fewer chances to recover from the day’s stress.
The World Bank report pointed out that 120 million people in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal live in locations where outdoor heat stress already exceeds theoretical coping limits for at least one month annually. It highlighted a cost-benefit analysis, which found that heat early warning systems in Indian cities return roughly $50 for every $1 spent on them. Based on this, the report argued that authorities can protect residents and keep local economies working through the hottest months of the year by strengthening preparedness and response at the subnational level.
“In future decades, physiological and behavioral adaptation will undoubtedly help South Asians cope as heat stress levels rise. But the pace and scale of projected warming will increasingly test the limits of individual adaptation,” said the World Bank report.
Recently, the Indian government added heat waves to the list of natural calamities. This can help the government access funds for sustainable development goals (SDG). A policy framework for providing relief assistance through state and federal disaster response fund is being prepared, the government told Parliament in August. Heat Wave Mitigation Projects are now eligible under the Disaster Mitigation Funds, it added.
Rights activists, however, point out a crucial gap — labor laws in South Asian countries neither set any temperature threshold for safe work nor recognize heatstroke or kidney disease as occupational illnesses worthy of compensation. The IIED report on Bangladesh calls for heat protection at work to become a binding legal requirement.
Such steps could prove useful for the entire South Asian workforce.

articles.title: The Thai Government’s Myanmar Gambit Could Backfire on ASEAN
articles.full_text:
Bangkok’s recent campaign of diplomatic outreach undermines the bloc’s collective approach to the country’s crisis.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul shakes hands with Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing in Bangkok, Thailand, Aug. 6, 2026.
On August 6, Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul rolled out the red carpet for Myanmar’s military-appointed leader Min Aung Hlaing. During the two-day visit, Anutin pledged to work with Myanmar to eventually reintegrate the country into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has excluded it from its summits since late 2021. The two countries also signed three memoranda of understanding in labor, water, and space cooperation during the visit. Min Aung Hlaing also visited the Thai parliament and invited Thai business leaders to invest in the war-torn country.
The invitation to Min Aung Hlaing was opposed by Thai civil societies and activist networks. Most notable is the protest by a Thai MP who shouted calls for peace and humanity during his appearance in the parliament. For the junta leader, the trip served as a major diplomatic win due to the relative diplomatic isolation that he has faced since the military coup of 2021.
Obviously, Thailand is the foreign country most directly impacted by Myanmar’s civil war, from massive inflow of legal and illegal migrants into the country to cross-border crime and scam networks. Thus, it is understandable that Thailand would want to work to reduce tensions within Myanmar, especially the Thai-Myanmar border, and to promote peace and stability.
What is significant and puzzling is its increasing divergence from ASEAN in addressing the crisis. By officially inviting Min Aung Hlaing to visit Thailand, the Thai government has arguably lent legitimacy to the junta leader without requiring any efforts at implementing ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus. As Professor Thitinan Pongsudhirak from Chulalongkorn University recently argued, this not only diverges from the ASEAN approach to the conflict but also creates difficulties for the Philippines, the current ASEAN chair, and for Singapore, which will take ASEAN’s helm in 2027.
Why Thailand is adopting such a unilateral and divergent approach from its ASEAN counterparts is muddled. On one hand, Thailand is optimistic that what it refers to as “calibrated reengagement” towards Myanmar will eventually yield concessions and cooperation from Myanmar’s side. Citing detained leader Daw Aung San Suu Kyi’s recent meeting with a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross, Anutin claimed that the situation in the country is moving in the right direction. Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow also stated that Myanmar would undertake further positive steps and allow ASEAN representatives to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi.
Thailand is thus trying to advocate a softer and more accommodative approach to Myanmar. In doing so, they claim that their approach is more effective or would yield positive results in the near future. This also reflects Thailand’s growing impatience with the ongoing situation in Myanmar and with ASEAN’s approach to the conflict. The Thai government’s move could be interpreted as a conclusion that ASEAN’s stance of excluding the junta leader and his government from the bloc’s summits made the latter increasingly uncooperative, limiting ASEAN’s ability to persuade it to make concessions, such as the release of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi and the resumption of inclusive political dialogue.
Thailand’s incongruent, if not contradictory, approach to Myanmar’s conflict with ASEAN has broader implications and consequences beyond its strong urge to resolve the crisis along its western border. Ultimately, it could undermine and challenge ASEAN’s collective approach to the crisis. Despite growing dissatisfaction towards ASEAN by both outsiders and the Burmese public in handling the crisis and the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, ASEAN has taken several unprecedented steps, most notably the exclusion of the military leaders and political appointees from high-level summits and ministerial meetings.
According to some analysts, ASEAN has been undertaking some creative reinterpretations of its founding principle of non-interference, while simultaneously adhering to it. It has framed the Myanmar conflict as having “adversely impacted regional stability,” implying that the crisis is not merely an internal affair, while also acknowledging that the solutions must be “Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led.” Successive ASEAN chairs have broadly held the same line, despite slight shifts in approaches from year to year, demonstrating consistency and consensus in the bloc’s position.
In this regard, even though Thailand claims to adhere to the Five-Point Consensus, its recent policy of calibrated reengagement with Myanmar’s military-appointed government, and its most recent invitation to Min Aung Hlaing onto Thai soil, without progress in the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, is a direct challenge to ASEAN unity. Just recently, the ASEAN special envoy on Myanmar, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said that Myanmar’s readmission to ASEAN was still “far off” without significant progress in the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus. This explicitly contradicts Thailand’s pledge to reintegrate Myanmar into ASEAN. Meanwhile, Myanmar has shown no intention to make progress on the Consensus; indeed, it has openly criticized it. Thailand’s unilateral approach also undermines the bloc’s unified position on the crisis, as two observably different approaches are now running in parallel.
The effectiveness of Thailand’s approach will be tested over time, although there is little hope of achieving genuine peace and stability by accommodating the military-appointed government and by excluding various stakeholders, particularly the revolutionary groups and ethnic organizations, from engagement. At the same time, Thailand’s Myanmar gambit tests ASEAN’s consensus on the crisis and may, in the longer term, erode ASEAN’s role as a regional actor in promoting peace and stability.

This explicitly contradicts Thailand’s pledge to reintegrate Myanmar into ASEAN. Meanwhile, Myanmar has shown no intention to make progress on the Consensus; indeed, it has openly criticized it. Thailand’s unilateral approach also undermines the bloc’s unified position on the crisis, as two observably different approaches are now running in parallel.
The effectiveness of Thailand’s approach will be tested over time, although there is little hope of achieving genuine peace and stability by accommodating the military-appointed government and by excluding various stakeholders, particularly the revolutionary groups and ethnic organizations, from engagement. At the same time, Thailand’s Myanmar gambit tests ASEAN’s consensus on the crisis and may, in the longer term, erode ASEAN’s role as a regional actor in promoting peace and stability.
On August 6, Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul rolled out the red carpet for Myanmar’s military-appointed leader Min Aung Hlaing. During the two-day visit, Anutin pledged to work with Myanmar to eventually reintegrate the country into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has excluded it from its summits since late 2021. The two countries also signed three memoranda of understanding in labor, water, and space cooperation during the visit. Min Aung Hlaing also visited the Thai parliament and invited Thai business leaders to invest in the war-torn country.
The invitation to Min Aung Hlaing was opposed by Thai civil societies and activist networks. Most notable is the protest by a Thai MP who shouted calls for peace and humanity during his appearance in the parliament. For the junta leader, the trip served as a major diplomatic win due to the relative diplomatic isolation that he has faced since the military coup of 2021.
Thu Htet is a DPhil candidate in Southeast Asian Studies at the University of Oxford, where he previously completed an MPhil in International Relations. His research focuses on Southeast Asian international relations and the foreign policies of regional states.
articles.summary: Bangkok's recent campaign of diplomatic outreach undermines the bloc's collective approach to the country's crisis.

articles.title: Bou Meng, Survivor of Khmer Rouge Security Prison, Dies Aged 85
articles.full_text:
The painter was one of 14,000-plus men, women, and children who were sent to S-21 between 1975 and 1979 – and one of just a handful to survive.
Bou Meng sells copies of his autobiography at Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Mar. 17, 2013.
The Cambodian artist Bou Meng, one of the few known survivors of the notorious S-21 security prison in Phnom Penh, has died at the age of 85, severing another living connection to the worst atrocities of the Khmer Rouge.
The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), a U.N.-backed tribunal that has tried a handful of former Khmer Rouge leaders for genocide and other crimes against humanity, said in a statement that Bou Meng died at 11:00 p.m. on Friday “due to age-related illness.”
“The passing of Mr. Bou Meng represents the loss of an important historical witness to the grave crimes committed during the brutal Khmer Rouge regime, particularly to the history and tragedy that took place at the former S-21 Security Centre,” the ECCC stated.
Bou Meng was one of 14,000-plus men, women, and children who were sent to S-21 during the 1975-1979 rule of Democratic Kampuchea, as the Khmer Rouge state was officially known. After taking power in April 1975, the Khmer Rouge made a mad dash towards agrarian utopia, emptying most of the cities and towns, and putting Cambodians to work on grim rural labor communes. During its three years, and eight months, and 20 days in power, the Khmer Rouge caused the deaths of an estimated 1.7 million people, through disease, starvation, and execution.
S-21, also known as Tuol Sleng, was built in a high school in the southern suburbs of Phnom Penh and served as the nerve-center of the regime’s fearsome security apparatus. Nearly all of those sent to S-21 were interrogated, forced to sign mostly false confessions, and then executed at a “killing field” on the city’s outskirts. Only seven adult prisoners were known to have got out alive.
As he recounts in his memoir, “Bou Meng: A Survivor From Khmer Rouge Prison S-21,” in 1977, Meng was arrested and accused of spying for the United States and held for two years at S-21. Like Vann Nath, another artist who survived S-21, Meng escaped execution only because of his skill as a painter, and was put to work producing propaganda portraits of the Khmer Rouge leader, “Brother Number One” Pol Pot, and other officials. However, this did little to save his wife Ma Yoeun and two children, all of whom perished under the Khmer Rouge.
Bou Meng, along with Vann Nath and Chum Mey, a mechanic, were spared because he could repair the prison’s sewing machines, testified in 2009 at the ECCC trial of Kaing Guek Eav, aka Comrade Duch, a former schoolteacher who served as the prison’s commandant.
During his testimony, Meng recalled the torture he experienced after his arrival in Tuol Sleng. He told the court that prisoners were kept in chains with empty bullet boxes and plastic bottles to use as toilet.
“I saw about 20 men with long hair, looking very sick and emaciated. The cell was like hell on earth,” Meng told the court. “I saw a lizard and hoped it would drop on me so I could catch it and eat it,” he added. “They kept whipping me and asked me when I joined the CIA.”
Meng was given a lifeline when S-21 officials sought a painter among the detainees to produce a portrait of Pol Pot. He continued to work as an artist until S-21 was liberated by the Vietnamese military after it overthrew the Khmer Rouge in January 1979.
In July 2010, the ECCC found Duch guilty of crimes against humanity and war crimes as well as homicide and torture, and sentenced him to 35 years in prison. In early 2012, a Supreme Court Chamber upheld the conviction, upping his sentence to life imprisonment. Duch died in 2022 at the age of 77.
His testimony, which was also cited in the tribunal’s second case, made a “significant contribution to the pursuit of truth and justice for victims,” the ECCC said in its statement.
In his later years, Bou Meng could often be seen at the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, the former site of S-21, where he sold copies of his memoir and spoke to visitors about his experiences.
Meng’s death leaves Chum Mey as the only living adult survivor of S-21.

articles.title: Joint Resource Exploration With China a ‘Possibility’ Before 2028, Philippine President Says
articles.full_text:
Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said that Manila and Beijing have made progress in energy talks, despite the ongoing tensions in the South China Sea.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. takes part in a luncheon with foreign journalists in Manila, Philippines, Aug. 14, 2026.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. says that joint offshore oil and gas exploration with China remains a “distinct possibility” before the end of his term in 2028, despite the recent intensification of their disputes in the South China Sea.
Speaking at a foreign media luncheon in Manila on Friday, Marcos said that Manila and Beijing were making progress in talks on the matter, and that the U.S.-Israel-Iran war had highlighted Manila’s need to shore up its energy security.
“The Philippines needs additional supplies of oil and gas, and we need to explore the possibilities that we have in the Philippines, in the West Philippine Sea, and wherever else we can [that] we can take advantage of,” he said, as per Rappler.
In March, Marcos told Bloomberg Television that the war in the Middle East and the resulting oil supply shock could provide an “impetus for both sides to come to an agreement” after years of friction in disputed waters. The interview aired on the same day that Marcos declared a “national energy emergency” due to the impacts of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which saw a sudden spike in fuel prices.
The two Asian countries then undertook “initial exchanges” on the topic during a meeting between diplomats in late March, which also involved discussions on how to manage disputes in the South China Sea.
“This discussion has gained prominence,” Marcos told reporters. “There were several issues from the beginning that we are slowly working through. And I can see the distinct possibility that there will be such joint explorations.”
Marcos did not mention when a deal could be reached, saying the discussions were still ongoing. “I think the sense that I get is that all parties involved want it to succeed, and that is always a very good sign,” he said.
Marcos’ predecessor Rodrigo Duterte terminated oil and gas exploration talks with China in mid-2022, with then-Foreign Secretary Teodoro Locsin saying that discussions had gone as far as “it is constitutionally possible to go.”
Marcos and Chinese leader Xi Jinping agreed to resume them during Marcos’ state visit to Beijing in early 2023, but have made very little progress due to the intensification of the disputes in the South China Sea. Since taking office, Marcos has openly challenged China’s behavior in Philippine-claimed waters, fortifying security relations with the United States and introducing a “transparency” policy that focused on publicizing the aggressive actions of the China Coast Guard in the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
As I noted at the time of Marcos’ initial comment, joint exploration of offshore resources (let alone joint development) remains unlikely at the current juncture. Despite Marcos’ call for a “reset” in relations, recent months have seen a rise in tensions between the CCG and Philippine Coast Guard and navy vessels in disputed waters, which culminated on July 20 in a physical altercation between Chinese and Philippine personnel at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands.
The Philippines said that one of its personnel sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by CCG personnel who had deployed in a boat close to the BRP Sierra Madre, the grounded warship that serves as Manila’s outpost on the shoal. China accused the Philippines of attempting to ram the Chinese boat, and of spreading “false propaganda” about the incident. This was followed by two confrontations at Scarborough Shoal, some 650 kilometers to the northeast.
The recent tensions appear to have grown out of the Philippine commemorations of the 10th anniversary of the arbitral ruling handed down by a court of arbitration in The Hague. The ruling found that China’s expansive “nine-dash line,” which asserts Beijing’s sovereignty over nearly all of the South China Sea, had no standing under international law. It also found that Second Thomas Shoal is part of the Philippines’ EEZ and continental shelf. China has dismissed the ruling as “null and void.”
Even if China and the Philippines could reach a deal on joint oil and gas exploration, this would have to surmount considerable constitutional and political hurdles in Manila.
The Philippine Constitution states that “the exploration, development, and utilization of natural resources must remain under the full control and supervision of the State, and may be undertaken only by the State itself or through Filipino citizens or corporations that are at least 60 percent Filipino-owned.”
After Marcos’ initial comment in March, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) stated that any future joint oil and gas exploration with China would “be made solely in accordance with the Philippine Constitution and the country’s laws, jurisprudence and regulations, and in full assertion of its sovereign prerogatives.”

articles.title: How China Is Normalizing Its Presence in the Waters East of Taiwan
articles.full_text:
Accidents, the ‘normalization’ of law enforcement and integration into a sphere of influence
Following the Japan-Philippines Summit Meeting on May 28, 2026, Japan and the Philippines are to hold negotiations to determine the boundaries of their overlapping Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) and continental shelves in the waters east of Taiwan. The main goals include clarifying the scope of resource development, strengthening defense and maritime security cooperation, and preventing unforeseen clashes. Japan regards this as a model of peaceful resolution under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and consistent with international law; China strongly protests the initiative. Since China considers Taiwan part of its own territory, it claims rights over the waters east of the island and objects that Japan and the Philippines should not negotiate boundaries without Chinese involvement.
China has long argued for the legitimacy of the nine-dash line in the South China Sea, asserting that the islands and waters of the South China Sea are Chinese territory. Less noted is that the northeastern end of the nine-dash line runs along southeastern Taiwan, and the “2023 edition of China’s standard map,” published by the Ministry of Natural Resources on August 28, 2023, adds a tenth dash line east of Taiwan. This confirms China’s strong interest in those waters. China has also deployed carrier groups there and repeatedly conducted exercises suggesting preparation for an invasion of Taiwan from the east.
As China’s interest in the waters east of Taiwan grew, the People’s Liberation Army commenced activities there. Then, in June 2026, China criticized Japan and the Philippines at the same moment the China Coast Guard (CCG) began conducting law enforcement patrols off Taiwan’s eastern coast. It has kept those patrols going in an effort to normalize them. Military, legal, and administrative functions are now acting in concert.
These recent actions are reminiscent of the Kinmen Islands episode in February 2024. On February 14, after two Chinese fishermen died during a crackdown by the Taiwanese Coast Guard near Kinmen, the CCG abruptly announced it would conduct law enforcement patrols in the Xiamen-Kinmen waters and declared such activities would be normalized, effectively breaking boundaries Taiwan had set and forcing a very real change in the status quo. The Kinmen episode was not the first such instance. The same applies to the Senkaku Islands: in September 2012, when the Japanese government purchased and nationalized private land there, Beijing responded by routinely allowing coast guard vessels to intrude into Senkaku territorial waters as a form of law enforcement. China has thus made it a routine approach to exploit incidents and accidents, voice protests, normalize previously non-existent law enforcement activities, and change the status quo.
This time, the opening of boundary negotiations between Japan and the Philippines is being treated as an “incident or accident,” prompting the CCG to commence and normalize hitherto unseen law enforcement activities off Taiwan’s eastern coast. Based on the Senkaku and Kinmen precedents, those activities can be expected to become normalized and conducted on a daily basis.
Since Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s remarks about the “situation threatening national survival” at the House of Representatives Budget Committee on November 7, 2025, China has ramped up its criticism of Japan, framing all of Tokyo’s foreign policy as “neo-militarism.” Under the guise of protesting this, China continues to litigate Japanese responsibility while simultaneously changing the status quo. The narrative propagated domestically and internationally, of course, is that Japan and others moved first, thereby justifying Chinese actions. This is a pattern likely to keep recurring in the Western Pacific.

articles.title: Indonesia Is the Latest Country to Validate China’s Claim to Taiwan – Unwittingly or Not
articles.full_text:
From Indonesia to Africa and Oceania, China is enlisting foreign countries to support its increasingly strict interpretation of the One China principle.
On the morning of August 12, China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and an Indonesian Navy warship conducted a joint navigation exercise in the waters east of Taiwan. It was the first time China had exercised with a foreign military in these geopolitically sensitive waters.
The announcement a day earlier had drawn a swift rebuke from Taiwan’s authorities, which called the exercise an act of political manipulation, “aimed at creating a false impression before the international community that the Chinese communists have jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan.” The United States similarly called on China “to cease its continuous military pressure against Taiwan.”
Chinese state media indeed framed the exercises as evidence of its jurisdiction over the area. The Global Times, a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party, quoted Chinese military affairs expert Zhang Junshe describing the exercise as being of “great significance,” both because it was the first of its kind and because it demonstrated “China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan island.”
The exercise came at a moment when Beijing has increased its operational presence in the waters east of Taiwan in an effort to assert its jurisdiction. After Japan and the Philippines agreed to start delimitation talks over their exclusive economic zones (EEZs), which overlap to the east of Taiwan, China sent Coast Guard and law enforcement vessels to patrol the disputed waters in early June. Although the PLAN has regularly held exercises in these waters, it marked the first time the Coast Guard patrolled the region independently. 
The Coast Guard presence, accompanied by law enforcement and research vessels, were framed as a routine expression of Beijing’s sovereignty over the area. Although initially a special operation, it has now become semi-permanent. And now China is roping in third countries to corroborate its jurisdiction, with state media making this link directly.
In turn, Indonesia’s Navy downplayed the significance of the exercise. Indonesian media reported that the navy confirmed a “limited joint training or passing exercises” with the PLAN on its way back from a joint exercise with Russia in Vladivostok. It added that the vessel in question also conducted similar exercises with Japan’s navy and the U.S. Navy’s Seventh Fleet. 
The press statement seemed to deliberately sidestep the question of jurisdiction, instead referring to Indonesia’s “free and active” foreign policy and the “universal naval tradition conducted when transiting through another country’s maritime area.” A later statement dropped the “country” reference, simply stating “a maritime area” instead. 
It’s difficult to assess whether Indonesia was aware beforehand of the sensitivity of these drills. While Beijing emphasized the significance of the exercises, Jakarta called them routine.
The incident is more evidence of a recent trend where China enlists foreign countries to support its increasingly strict interpretation of the One China principle. The old playbook of China and Taiwan’s diplomatic competition focused on Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies and participation in international organizations: Since the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) won the Presidency in 2016, Taiwan has seen the number of diplomatic allies dwindle from 23 to 12. Despite those restrictions, Taipei has proven remarkably flexible and maintains unofficial relations with countries throughout the world. 
However, over the last year Beijing has become more strident in getting other countries to subscribe to its more strict interpretation of its One China principle. As a result, organizations throughout Africa, Oceania, and even in some Western countries have become more hesitant to engage with any official institutions or documents that bear the name Taiwan, or its official name: the Republic of China.
The most notable example of this happened in April, when the Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar revoked overflight clearance to block President Lai Ching-te’s trip to Eswatini, citing their lack of recognition of Taiwan. Although overseas visits have caused tensions between Taiwan and China before, it was the first time third countries were so directly involved in blocking a visit. 
Taiwan’s presidential office blamed Chinese economic coercion. More likely, as the Global South Project argued, these countries spotted an easy opportunity to win points with Beijing, who indeed thanked the countries for abiding by the One-China principle. Eventually, Lai did visit Eswatini after being smuggled in on an Eswatini government airplane. 
Other African countries have also hardened their policies on Taiwan. In June, Kenya confiscated the passports of two Taiwanese academics who traveled there to participate in the Our Oceans Conference, declaring it doesn’t recognize ROC passports. A month earlier, Zambia cancelled RightsCon 2026, a major human rights conference. The organizer cited Chinese pressure over the participation of Taiwanese civil society members. In July, Morocco announced it stopped processing visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese passport holders, causing Taiwanese travelers to cancel their planned visits. Finally, this week, Ugandan officials withheld the passports of several Taiwanese travelers and demanded Chinese passports instead, explicitly citing Uganda’s “One China policy.” In response, Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a travel advisory for Uganda. 
While some of the passport issues were later clarified, the closure of Taipei’s representative office in Papua New Guinea seems to be permanent. In July, Papua New Guinea’s Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko abruptly announced the closure of Taiwan’s representative office in Port Moresby to align with the One China policy. Beijing welcomed the decision in a statement published before the official announcement.
The issues of Taiwanese citizens and organizations in Africa and Oceania are examples of China’s grey-zone pressure on Taiwan going global. Under the old playbook, diplomatic switches were clearly attributable to China. Passing exercises, visa issues, and passport quirks are more deniable and reversible; they make it difficult for Taipei to put the blame on a single actor, while Beijing gets international validation that the Republic of China does not exist.
This strategy also has its limits. The Indonesian Navy perhaps did not anticipate becoming a pawn in Beijing’s game, but by refusing to take a clear side it still allowed China to frame the exercise as an endorsement. As a Taiwanese intelligence officer said, “Militarily this does not have a direct impact on Taiwan. It has a geopolitical significance.” While Indonesia gently pushed back, would the next country do the same?
