That potential should not be overstated, however. Vietnam’s rare-earth industry remains in its infancy; the country has limited refining capacity, and existing facilities remain concentrated in relatively basic stages of processing. Vietnam Rare Earths operates the country’s only light rare-earth refining facility in Ha Nam province, with an annual capacity of just 5,000 tonnes. Vietnam still lacks the scale of separation and downstream capabilities required for a fully integrated supply chain.
The value of these materials depends on the ability to mine, separate, refine and transform them into inputs for advanced manufacturing. Vietnam’s policy is beginning to address this gap. An amendment to the Law on Geology and Minerals passed in December 2025 classifies rare earths as a “special strategic” mineral and places their exploration, mining, and processing under tighter state control. It also prohibits the export of raw rare-earth materials and places greater emphasis on domestic processing and higher-value products.
This is only partly a reaction to China’s latest export controls. Vietnam and Japan began cooperating on rare-earth development more than a decade ago. In 2010, the two countries agreed to cooperate on rare-earth exploration, mining and processing, including technology transfer and human-resource development, following the vulnerabilities exposed by the 2010 China-Japan rare-earth dispute. More recently, during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s visit to Vietnam in May, rare-earth development and supply-chain cooperation were again highlighted as strategically important to Japan’s economic security.
Recent corporate investment shows how Vietnam’s manufacturing and critical-mineral stories are beginning to intersect. South Korea’s Star Group Industrial operates a magnet plant in Quang Nam Province that was developed with an investment of $80 million and has sought alternative rare-earth supplies from Vietnam and Australia. Chinese magnet producer Baotou INST Magnetic, which was added to Apple’s supplier list in 2021, also expanded into Vietnam in 2023 in response to pressure from its customers, who pushed it to diversify production beyond China.
These examples show that supply-chain diversification is starting to move beyond manufacturing. Magnet manufacturers have an incentive to locate closer to electronics and automotive companies already operating in Vietnam, while Vietnam’s existing manufacturing base creates potential downstream demand. The connection, however, remains incomplete, due to the aforementioned limitations in supplying processed rare-earth minerals to these companies.
Vietnam’s broader industrial policy points in a similar direction. Its supporting-industry development program for 2026–2035 seeks to strengthen domestic production, increase localization, and deepen the participation of Vietnamese enterprises in global supply chains. The government aims to raise average localization rates in key industries to 40–45 percent by 2030.
Together, the mineral law and the supporting-industry program reflect Vietnam’s broader ambition to capture more value from the country’s raw materials. It will not be easy. China’s dominance in rare earths has been built through decades of investment in processing technologies, industrial infrastructure, downstream manufacturing, and integrated supply chains. Vietnam’s current capabilities remain far more limited, particularly in separation, refining, and downstream production. The challenge is whether greater diversification by foreign companies can gradually expand the country’s own rare-earth processing and manufacturing capabilities.
The China Plus One trend has helped expand Vietnam’s manufacturing base, attract foreign investment and integrate it more deeply into global production networks. It has also created a growing base of electronics, automotive, and other manufacturing activities that depend on critical inputs such as rare-earth magnets. As companies look to diversify those upstream supplies, Vietnam’s rare-earth resources could become more relevant to the country’s position in global supply chains. Whether it can build the capacity to extract and process these materials will help determine how far Vietnam’s rare-earth resources can contribute to the next stage of China Plus One.
Over the past few years, China Plus One has reshaped global production, helping Vietnam emerge as an important manufacturing base. China Plus One involves companies reducing their excessive dependence on a single production base (i.e., China) by adding capacity elsewhere, which many have already done. However, the next stage of this strategy is likely to be more complicated. Export controls and economic security concerns are exposing vulnerabilities further upstream, particularly in industries that depend on critical minerals. This has demonstrated that even if a company can diversify where it manufactures, it may remain dependent on concentrated supplies of the materials, components, and processing capabilities necessary for that production.
Vietnam illustrates this challenge particularly well. China Plus One has brought major investments and increasingly sophisticated manufacturing activities to the country. Amkor Technology, for example, has invested $1.6 billion in a semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging facility in Bac Ninh province outside Hanoi. Such investments have deepened Vietnam’s links to technologically intensive global supply chains and have made the security of critical inputs increasingly relevant to the country’s economy.
Tran Thi Mong Tuyen is a Fellow at the Pacific Forum, a Rotary Scholar, and a PhD candidate at National Chengchi University
articles.summary: Vietnam has benefited greatly from foreign firms' desire to de-risk from China. Can it free itself of dependence on the country's critical rare earth inputs?

articles.title: Myanmar’s Resistance Finally Has a Unified Front
articles.full_text:
The new Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union could change the course of the country’s conflict.
Civil defense trainees attend a graduation ceremony for a capacity building program run by the Defense Ministry of Myanmar’s National Unity Government in Sagaing Region, Myanmar, Apr. 19, 2026.
I was serving as Dean of the University of Medicine in Yangon when Myanmar’s military staged its coup in February 2021. Overnight, I became an activist in the resistance movement, serving in a variety of roles. Like millions of my fellow citizens, I joined peaceful protests and helped lead the Civil Disobedience Movement.
My involvement soon made me a wanted man, forcing me to flee to a neighboring country before I eventually received refuge in Europe. I was later appointed minister of health and education in the National Unity Government (NUG), which was formed in April 2021 to lead the resistance to the coup.
Since then, throughout what has become known as the Myanmar Spring Revolution, I have witnessed both its triumphs and its setbacks firsthand. Living abroad also allowed me to engage extensively with foreign governments and Myanmar diaspora communities before I returned to Myanmar in 2025. I am now based in one of Myanmar’s liberated areas – territories under the control of revolutionary forces.
Against this backdrop, I believe the recent creation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF) represents the most significant turning point in Myanmar’s resistance movement since the 2021 coup.
Some have dismissed the SCEF as merely another acronym. Nothing could be further from the truth. It represents one of the most consequential political and military realignments in Myanmar’s modern history. It addresses one of the central weaknesses that has long undermined Myanmar’s democratic struggle: the inability of anti-military forces to sustain a unified political and military front across ethnic and ideological lines.
The Steering Council brings together several of Myanmar’s most powerful and politically significant resistance actors, including the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO), the Karen National Union (KNU), the Chin National Front (CNF), the Karenni, the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the exile parliamentary body, and the NUG. Such broad participation is unprecedented.
For decades, Myanmar’s ethnic resistance organizations (EROs) understood that none could defeat the military on their own. Yet repeated attempts to build durable alliances collapsed under the weight of mistrust, competing interests, ethnic divisions, and external pressures. At the same time, many EROs came to recognize that their remarkable battlefield successes since 2021 would not have been possible without the nationwide Spring Revolution, which fundamentally transformed Myanmar’s political landscape.
One major attempt at unity followed the 1988 uprising with the creation of the Democratic Alliance of Burma, which brought together the KNU, the KIO, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front, and several other organizations around a shared federal vision. The alliance fractured in 1994 after the KIO signed a ceasefire agreement with the junta. Subsequent ERO coalitions were more limited in scope, focusing primarily on military coordination and territorial defense rather than the development of an inclusive federal political framework that incorporated the Bamar-majority democratic movement.
The Steering Council is different from previous alliances because it integrates political leadership with military coordination. It unites long-established ethnic armed organizations with the post-coup democratic resistance led by the NUG and the CRPH. In doing so, it also addresses the question that I have been repeatedly asked during meetings with foreign officials: whether Myanmar’s anti-junta movement can evolve into a coherent national alternative rather than remain a loose collection of armed groups pursuing divergent political objectives. Some feared that the collapse of military rule might produce fragmentation resembling the post-conflict experiences of Libya or Syria. The emergence of the Steering Council should go a long way toward alleviating those concerns.
The formation of the SCEF has been several years in the making. Discussions began during confidential meetings in Europe in October 2022 and continued through a series of negotiations inside Myanmar and across neighboring countries. This slow and deliberate process reflected the difficulty of building trust among organizations with different political cultures, military structures, and historical grievances.
As an initial step, on January 31, 2024, the CNF, KNU, Karenni, and NUG issued the Joint Position Statement Towards the Annihilation of Military Dictatorship and the Establishment of a Federal Democratic Union. Informally known as the K2C–NUG Position Statement, the document outlined six political objectives that closely resemble those of the Steering Council. The KIO’s formal participation in the Steering Council represents a major breakthrough in coalition-building and provides a roadmap for the eventual inclusion of additional ethnic organizations.
Discussions are also underway with several other EROs. While understandings and frameworks for future collaboration are being developed, the sensitive nature of these negotiations prevents any further public disclosure at this stage.
The Steering Council is the product of years of patient negotiations and incremental consensus-building, making it more likely to endure than previous alliances. Its institutional design also reflects a level of organizational maturity that earlier coalitions lacked. The SCEF has been deliberately structured as a long-term institution capable of leading both wartime resistance and the subsequent political transition.
At the SCEF’s apex is a Strategic Leadership Committee composed of seven senior representatives, one from each member organization. Beneath it operates a Secretariat consisting of 12 senior officials empowered to make operational decisions without constant referral to their respective organizations. This is a deliberate effort to streamline coordination within a movement often criticized for fragmentation and slow decision-making. I serve as one of those 12 Secretariat members.
Supporting the Secretariat are committees responsible for foreign affairs, finance, federal affairs, security, and interior affairs. Resources and funding are intended to be shared equitably, while the Steering Council seeks to present itself internationally as a unified body speaking with one voice.
Alongside the Secretariat is the Military Affairs Coordinating Body, composed of ten senior commanders from member organizations responsible for military operations, procurement, and logistics. It reports directly to the Strategic Leadership Committee.
In effect, the Steering Council institutionalizes what Myanmar’s resistance has historically lacked: unified political leadership directly linked to coordinated military operations. For the first time since the 2021 coup, Myanmar’s principal democratic and ethnic resistance organizations have created a genuinely integrated political and military framework with national ambitions.
Myanmar’s resistance landscape remains extraordinarily complex, and powerful external actors could still complicate efforts to expand or consolidate the coalition. The alliance’s members are fully aware of these challenges, and we understand that our credibility will ultimately depend on demonstrating effective battlefield coordination, measurable progress, and coherent diplomacy abroad.
Several Steering Council representatives have already visited foreign capitals to brief governments, with additional visits planned. Most recently, a briefing was held in Thailand for diplomats and representatives of selected civil society organizations. We have been encouraged by the positive response and optimism expressed by many participants.
The Military’s New Government Will Not Bring Peace
In April, following a widely discredited sham election in December and January, the junta has attempted to rebrand itself as a civilian government. The new president is none other than the former junta chief, while the ruling party remains dominated by former military officers and junta loyalists. This arrangement cannot bring genuine peace or stability because it runs contrary to the people’s aspirations for freedom, democracy, and equality among all ethnic communities.
The major EROs controlling large portions of the country are currently members of the Steering Council and have rejected the new government. The Arakan Army, which controls significant territory in western Myanmar, continues to wage major offensives against the military. Several other EROs governing extensive areas in northeastern Myanmar are not currently engaged in active fighting, despite their remarkable success during the Operation 1027 offensive in late 2023 and 2024, largely because of external pressure.
The claim that the new government, which controls only a handful of major urban centers, can bring peace and stability therefore does not withstand scrutiny. Myanmar is no longer governed exclusively from Naypyidaw. Across large parts of the country, ethnic resistance organizations already provide governance, including local administration, education, healthcare, and other public services.
The Steering Council is the clearest indication yet that Myanmar’s resistance is evolving from a reactive anti-coup movement into an increasingly organized national coalition capable of shaping a post-junta federal order.
In many respects, the Steering Council is laying the institutional foundations for the future state of Myanmar – a process that has repeatedly been interrupted repeatedly by military coups, fragile ceasefires, sham civilian governments, and periods of incomplete democratic rule since the country gained independence in 1948.
The Steering Council offers the people of Myanmar their best opportunity in decades to end military rule and replace perpetual conflict with a new political system capable of delivering lasting peace, security, freedom, democracy, and equality.
For the international community, it presents a rare opportunity to engage with a resistance movement that is increasingly coordinated, politically coherent, and committed to building a democratic federal union capable of bringing long-term stability and prosperity to Myanmar and the wider region.
I was serving as Dean of the University of Medicine in Yangon when Myanmar’s military staged its coup in February 2021. Overnight, I became an activist in the resistance movement, serving in a variety of roles. Like millions of my fellow citizens, I joined peaceful protests and helped lead the Civil Disobedience Movement.
articles.summary: The new Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union could change the course of the country's conflict.

articles.title: Japan’s Underground Lab Wants to Solve the World’s Nuclear Waste Problem
articles.full_text:
A rare visit to the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, where Japanese researchers are testing options for storing radioactive waste.
Scientists visiting the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory in Hokkaido, Japan.
Reindeer pastures and dairy farms stretch across the flat, windswept plain of Japan’s northernmost prefecture, giving little hint of what lies roughly 300 meters below. Inside the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, teams of engineers are trying to answer a question no country has fully solved: how to keep highly radioactive waste isolated from the environment for periods measured not in decades, but in tens of thousands of years.
In May, I gained special access to the facility through the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA), touring the underground galleries and observing several of the experiments currently underway.
Horonobe is one of only two underground research laboratories Japan has built to study geological disposal of high-level radioactive waste, and the only one still operating. Its counterpart, the Mizunami Underground Research Laboratory in Gifu Prefecture, was built in crystalline rock and was decommissioned in 2022 after its land lease expired. Horonobe, by contrast, sits in Neogene-era sedimentary rock, giving the JAEA a very different and, officials argue, complementary geological environment to study.
The project traces back to November 2000, when the governor of Hokkaido, the mayor of Horonobe town, and the president of the JAEA signed an agreement to permit research on the deep geological environment at the site. Construction and excavation followed over the next two decades, and the laboratory now includes shafts and galleries used to test how engineered barriers, groundwater, and surrounding rock interact over time – the same combination of natural and artificial safeguards that would, in theory, protect a real repository.
Two of the central experiments underway involve what the JAEA calls the “full-scale engineered barrier system performance experiment” and a “solute transport experiment,” both designed to test, at real scale, how bentonite buffers, canisters, and cement-based materials behave once water and pressure are introduced over years rather than months. The JAEA has also been testing how the surrounding sedimentary rock buffers natural disturbances, earthquakes, and groundwater shifts that could compromise a repository’s isolation over the long term.
The JAEA is emphatic on one point, repeated in nearly every briefing given to visitors: Horonobe is a research facility, not a candidate site for Japan’s eventual high-level waste repository. Japanese law formally separates the two functions, and the agency overseeing the actual site-selection process, the Nuclear Waste Management Organization of Japan, operates independently of the JAEA’s research program.
That legal separation has not entirely dissolved local unease. Horonobe is a farming town of roughly 2,000 residents, many of whom have lived for two decades with an underground laboratory in their backyard and, despite official assurances, the lingering question of what happens to the facility once the research concludes.
Japan’s broader search for a permanent repository has proven difficult everywhere it has been raised. Only two municipalities, Suttsu and Kamoenai in Hokkaido, have so far agreed even to preliminary literature-based surveys, and neither has committed to hosting a final site.
What distinguishes Horonobe today is its growing international role. In February 2023, the JAEA and the OECD’s Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) launched the Horonobe International Project, bringing foreign research organizations into the underground laboratory to work on shared technical problems. The first phase ran through March 2025 with 11 participating organizations from countries including Australia, Bulgaria, Germany, South Korea, Romania, Taiwan, and the United Kingdom, alongside Japan. 
A second phase, running from April 2025 through March 2029, has continued with roughly 10 member organizations pursuing three joint technical tasks: modeling how dissolved substances move through fractured sedimentary rock, integrating different repository design options, and dismantling a full-scale engineered barrier system to see how it performed after years underground.
For countries such as Australia and South Korea – both still in the early stages of building their own waste-management institutions – Horonobe offers something they cannot yet replicate at home: a working underground facility where design assumptions can be tested in real-world conditions. South Korea’s state nuclear research institute has said it is benchmarking its own disposal-performance models against Horonobe data as it prepares to build an underground laboratory of its own in Taebaek. 
NEA officials have described the site as an important international platform for developing and demonstrating repository technology, with plans to eventually extend the laboratory to 500 meters below sea level.
It is difficult to walk through Horonobe without thinking of Onkalo, the repository under construction on the island of Olkiluoto in western Finland, which is set to become the world’s first operational deep geological disposal site for spent nuclear fuel. Having visited Onkalo myself, the contrast with Horonobe is immediately clear. Onkalo is being excavated roughly 400 meters into Precambrian granite bedrock nearly 1.9 billion years old – rock that geologists consider to have remained structurally stable through repeated glacial cycles. Horonobe, by design, tests young, still-consolidating Neogene sedimentary rock, chosen precisely because it represents a geological setting Japan cannot avoid when it eventually has to site a real repository. Much of the country lacks Finland’s kind of ancient crystalline bedrock.
The difference between the two sides is as much political as geological. Posiva Oy, the utility consortium that owns and operates Onkalo, spent roughly two decades developing its technical solution and benefited from a Finnish system in which nuclear waste responsibility stays under public oversight even where the industry itself is privately run, with the national regulator STUK maintaining permanent inspectors on site. That framework was paired with sustained public consultation and a compensation system for the host municipality, Eurajoki, that turned three decades of engagement into local acceptance rather than opposition. Waste is due to begin arriving at Onkalo in 2026, sealed in copper-and-bentonite canisters designed to maintain their integrity for roughly 100,000 years.
Japan, by contrast, has yet to find a single municipality willing to host a final repository, and Horonobe’s own officials go out of their way to stress that the laboratory is not a step toward designating the town as one. 
Finland’s example has not gone unnoticed in Tokyo: Japanese institutions are already among the countries cooperating with Posiva on adapting Finnish containment technology to different geological and regulatory contexts, a channel that runs alongside, but separately from, the JAEA’s own international partnerships through the Horonobe International Project.
That gap helps explain why Horonobe matters beyond Japan’s borders. It is not a repository and, officially, will never become one. But it is one of a small number of places on Earth where engineers can watch, in real time and at full scale, whether the technology underpinning every country’s nuclear waste strategy actually behaves the way computer models predict over years of exposure to rock, water, and pressure.

articles.title: Data of 15 Million Kazakhstanis Allegedly Leaked
articles.full_text:
A hacker claims to have stolen the data from Kazakhstan eGov service. The authorities are investigating the claim.
Hackers have allegedly posted the personal data of 15 million Kazakhstani citizens for sale on the dark web. If confirmed, this would mark the second major breach of Kazakhstani citizen data in a little over a year.
According to RFE/RL, the Mash Telegram channel, which the outlet characterized as linked to the Russian security forces, reported that hackers had put the personal data of 15 million Kazakhstani citizens up for sale on the dark web. The seller reportedly claimed to have obtained the data after hacking Kazakhstan’s eGov service. The file is apparently valued at around $32,000 and, the seller claims, contains passport information, phone numbers, email addresses, document scans, and website passwords.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development acknowledged the reports and is reviewing them. In a statement posted to Telegram, the ministry said, “At this time, there is no confirmed evidence of a breach of e-government information systems or that the database in question was obtained directly from eGov.” The ministry cited inconsistencies between the claim and the structure of the eGov platform.
Data breaches are a fact of modern life the world over. Governments, including Kazakhstan’s, have increasingly pushed to digitalize services. On the one hand, the elimination of physical paperwork and office visits speeds service delivery, eliminating layers of bureaucracy and opportunities for petty corruption. But on the other hand, e-government introduces new risks, can obscure decisionmaking, and provides novel opportunities for corruption and crime. 
This latest report of leaked citizen data is not the first breach. In June 2025, the SecuriXy.kz Telegram channel reported that an archive containing information on 16.3 million Kazakhstani citizens had been leaked. The files reportedly contained 15.8 million IINs (individual identification numbers), 17 million phone numbers, alongside full names, dates of birth, and addresses.
At the time, SecuriXy.kz reported, “Analysis shows that most of the records are dated 2022, but relevant data from 2023–2024 was also discovered in the archive. This means the leak is recent and poses a real threat. This data could be used for phishing, document forgery, attacks on eGov and mobile banking accounts, and phone fraud.”
The file was reportedly posted on a hacker forum for free download under the title “Residents of Kazakhstan 2024.”
In its initial reporting on the incident, RFE/RL cited cybersecurity experts as suggesting three possible sources: “semi-open government service APIs, hacking of poorly configured platforms, or unauthorized downloads from integration systems.”
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation, and Aerospace Industry – rebranded in  September 2025 as the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development – quickly announced an investigation. In July 2025, Kazakh government officials appeared to downplay the significance of the leak. In a statement carried in the Astana Times, the ministry said, “The inspections confirmed that there were no breaches of government information systems. It was established that the database circulated on the internet contained outdated information, current as of 2022. The data originated from previous leaks and was partially supplemented by users with access to the systems as part of their official duties.”
Incidentally, earlier in June 2025, Kazakh authorities had detained a network of more than 140 people allegedly engaged in the selling of personal data via Telegram. 
Kazakhstan is leaning into the supposed AI future. Astana declared 2026 the “Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence” and in late 2025 passed Central Asia’s first comprehensive AI law. In June, Kazakhstan signed a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird and Nvidia to build the Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz. Earlier, in May, a presidential decree that got little media attention at the time granted the National Security Committee (KNB) new responsibilities, including making the security agency a direct participant in the AI buildout.

articles.title: ‘Silence Is Not an Option’: The Quest to Bear Witness to China’s Uyghur Camps
articles.full_text:
“Heart Full of Light,” Kalbinur Sidik’s memoir, provides a first-hand account of the atrocities against the Uyghur people in Xinjiang.
Kalbinur Sidik addressing the 15th Annual Geneva Summit for Human Rights and Democracy on May 17, 2023.
“When evil-doing comes like falling rain, nobody calls out ‘stop!’ When crimes begin to pile up they become invisible.” 
German playwright Bertolt Brecht’s observation on the political apathy that engulfed Germany in the 1930s resonates with 21st century survivors of the Chinese state’s war against Uyghurs in its northwestern heartland, known by exiles as East Turkestan. 
Germany’s slide into fascism brought book burnings and arrests of “undesirables.” It lead step by step to antisemitism, concentration camps, torture, and death. That brutal history echoes today in Beijing’s campaign against the Turkic peoples of its western regions – and in the silence of a deaf world. Only those who have experienced the terror first-hand and survived to tell the tale can hope to describe its full horrors.
Kalbinur Sidik (formerly Romanized as Qelbinur Sidik) is one such rare eyewitness to what many nations have termed a genocide. Her ordeal as a teacher inside the camps drove her to the brink of collapse. She escaped in 2019 ostensibly for medical treatment, hoping to reunite with her daughter in the Netherlands and seek asylum. Speaking out became her path to healing. 
She told The Diplomat that “silence is not an option.” The faces of captives in her class have haunted her to this day. Since leaving, her mission has been to give voice to their silent cries.
Her memoir, “Heart Full of Light” – a title reflecting the meaning of her name, Kalbinur – is full of horror and sadness but also memory, dignity and resistance. It is a cry against erasure and a wake-up call to a world that has not been listening.
The book begins with a child immersed in Uyghur culture and belonging, but there was darkness from the start. Sidik grew up cowed by the humiliation of her parents during the Cultural Revolution, a stigma that her family never shook off. Teaching offered hope but the glass ceiling separating her and her colleagues from the dominant Han Chinese was impenetrable.
Fast forward to 2016 as Beijing’s drive to sinicize everything Uyghur intensified. Sidik watched culture, language, and religion dismantled. Neighborhoods were bulldozed for “progress.” Academics, writers, and artists vanished. Eventually, more than 1 million Uyghurs were corralled into a vast network of “re-education” camps. 
Many women aged 18-50, including Sidik, were summoned for forced sterilization. Uyghur children were taken to boarding schools, and 1 million Han cadres were dispersed to “pair up and become family” with Uyghur households; to eat, study and sleep with them to further ethnic harmony. Her husband’s boss volunteered to billet with them, but his sexual advances made daily life intolerable.
2017 sealed the fate of Uyghur language education. Uyghur teachers were demoted, and replaced by Chinese counterparts. Disappearances escalated. Trust broke down. Spies were everywhere.
On February 28, 2017, Sidik was given a “top secret” assignment outside the city. Failure to report for duty or breach secrecy, would have consequences for her daughter in the Netherlands. “We know where she lives,” Sidik was told.
She arrived at gates bristling with soldiers, watchtowers, and cameras. A corridor of locked doors led to her “classroom,” filled with 100 child-sized stools.
Her “students,” young and old, shuffled in, shackled at the wrists and ankles connected by a chain. Sidik remembered shaved heads, lice, and the smell of squalor. Some wept quietly as they began rudimentary Mandarin. Finishing textbooks might earn freedom, they thought.
“Somehow, by the grace of God I stopped myself from curling up in a ball and weeping like a baby,” Sidik wrote. “Why me? Who are these people? Why are they locked up? What is this place?” Two cameras bore down on the classroom, and she dared not speak.
The reward for a morning’s study: a single steamed bun and watery gruel. That pattern would be repeated every day.
She called it the “most difficult day in 27 years of teaching.” She went home and wept uncontrollably.
Worse followed. House to house raids were relentless. Thousands poured into her camp. Cells for 10 held 50. Prisoners slept in shifts. Doors were chained above knee height, forcing men to crawl out. “The stench of urine and excretion was overwhelming.”
“Uyghurs are strong but their lice are stronger!” the guards mocked while boiling prisoner clothes as vermin floated to the surface.
Every week there were mysterious injections and blood tests. Inmates were pulled from class for interrogation and torture. Screams echoed until they stopped.
Every inch of the compound was monitored. If someone moved, a screen flashed red and zoomed in. “It was impossible not to compare them to animals in cages,” Sidik wrote of her students. “There was nowhere to hide. For them, or for me.”
The specter of organ harvesting hung over everything. Healthy young prisoners disappeared. Across Xinjiang authorities collected biodata from everyone aged 16-65. Mandatory DNA tests, bloods, iris scans, voice and gait recordings filled vast data banks, many believed for organ matching. Research later identified Saudis and Gulf Arabs traveling to eastern China for halal organs. 
“Alive we were worthless, dead, and cut up, our organs were worth a ransom,” Sidik wrote.
There was no one to confide in. Sidik took refuge in prayer, though it was banned. She planned suicide but thought of her daughter. Still, she stockpiled pills to take in case security forces knocked on the door one night. 
“I was not going to die being tortured,” she wrote.
When her six month contract ended, it was cause for relief – but heartbreak too. She was forbidden to say goodbye. 
“I can still picture each face. I was their hope in that dark place,” Sidik wrote.
Her good behavior earned her no respite. She was posted again, this time to a former nursing home crammed with thousands of women and girls. 
There were no showers. Clothing crawled with parasites. Women slept in turns on wooden boards in cells  holding 40-plus people.
articles.summary: “Heart Full of Light,” Kalbinur Sidik’s memoir, provides a first-hand account of the atrocities against the Uyghur people in Xinjiang.

articles.title: Takaichi, the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, and a Strained US Nuclear Umbrella
articles.full_text:
For Japan, the most immediate question is not whether to pursue nuclear weapons itself, but whether to allow its ally’s nuclear-capable assets on Japanese soil.
Eighty-one years after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, and Nagasaki on August 9, Japan is confronting an increasingly difficult contradiction: how to uphold its identity as the only country to have suffered atomic attack in wartime while strengthening deterrence against an increasingly formidable group of nuclear-armed neighbors.
The dilemma came into sharper focus during this year’s Hiroshima and Nagasaki commemorations. Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae stated that Japan “maintains” its Three Non-Nuclear Principles and reaffirmed Tokyo’s commitment to pursuing a world free of nuclear weapons. Yet when asked whether the principles would continue to be explicitly affirmed in the three strategic documents her government plans to revise by the end of the year, Takaichi declined to prejudge the wording.
That ambiguity matters. Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles – not possessing, not producing, and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japanese territory – trace back to former Prime Minister Sato Eisaku’s 1967 declaration and have long stood as a symbol of Japan’s postwar identity.
The tension was particularly visible in Nagasaki on August 9. Mayor Suzuki Shiro described nuclear weapons as an “absolute evil,” warned of the dangers of relying on nuclear deterrence, and urged the government to uphold the Three Non-Nuclear Principles. Takaichi, by contrast, reiterated Japan’s current adherence to the principles while emphasizing a “realistic and practical” approach toward achieving a world without nuclear weapons.
The strategic backdrop underpinning the Three Non-Nuclear Principles has shifted considerably. China is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear forces, North Korea continues to develop nuclear weapons and increasingly sophisticated missiles, and Russia remains one of the world’s two largest nuclear powers while deepening military cooperation with both Beijing and Pyongyang.
At the same time, doubts about the credibility of U.S. extended nuclear deterrence have grown harder to dismiss. Jennifer Lind and Daryl G. Press argued in Foreign Affairs this summer that the traditional U.S. nuclear umbrella is coming under increasing strain as adversaries acquire more credible means of striking the U.S. homeland. Their argument revives a long-standing concern about “decoupling”: whether Washington would risk devastating retaliation against the United States in order to defend an ally such as Japan or South Korea.
Put more starkly, the question is this: Would an American president risk Los Angeles to defend Tokyo or Seoul?
Under an “America First” posture in Washington, that question carries added political weight. The credibility of extended deterrence ultimately depends on whether an adversary believes Washington would accept the risk of nuclear retaliation to defend an ally.

Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro has argued that nuclear issues can no longer simply be avoided in policy discussions. Former Joint Staff Chief Kawano Katsutoshi has similarly questioned whether Japan can indefinitely assume that the American nuclear umbrella will hold, calling for a broader national debate.
Takaichi herself raised the underlying issue well before becoming prime minister. In a 2024 book, she revealed that, as a Cabinet minister in 2022, she had objected to language in the National Security Strategy stating that Japan’s basic policy of adhering to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles would remain unchanged.
Takaichi argued that if Japan expected U.S. extended deterrence to remain credible, the third principle – “not permitting the introduction” of nuclear weapons – was unrealistic. She wrote that she ultimately signed off on the Cabinet decision reluctantly after her request to remove the language was rejected.
That history gives greater significance to her carefully chosen wording in Hiroshima and Nagasaki this year.
The tension could become more concrete in the early 2030s. The U.S. Navy is developing a nuclear-armed Sea-Launched Cruise Missile, or SLCM-N, for integration aboard Virginia-class attack submarines. Tokyo will eventually have to ask whether strict adherence to “not permitting the introduction” is compatible with port visits by U.S. platforms potentially carrying such weapons, particularly if Washington maintains its traditional policy of neither confirming nor denying their presence.
The dilemma already impacts Japan’s defense diplomacy. For example, France’s nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, the Charles de Gaulle, has never called at a Japanese port. During Operation Clemenceau 25, its 2024-2025 Indo-Pacific deployment, the carrier visited Indonesia, the Philippines, and Singapore – but not Japan. 
Its embarked Rafale M fighters are capable of carrying France’s nuclear-armed ASMP-A air-launched cruise missile, although Paris does not publicly confirm or deny whether nuclear weapons are present aboard its strategic platforms.
Rear Admiral Guillaume Pinget, then-commander of the French Pacific Command, told this author in a July interview that France respects Japan’s laws and regulations and does not regard them as limiting the bilateral defense partnership. But he stopped short of predicting whether the Charles de Gaulle would eventually visit Japan.
“If Japan invites France to come, we will see,” Pinget said.
The case illustrates the potential friction between Japan’s non-nuclear policy and the nuclear deterrence postures of its partners.
Abandoning the Three Non-Nuclear Principles hastily would carry substantial political and diplomatic costs. They remain closely tied to Hiroshima and Nagasaki and underpin Japan’s credibility in advocating global nuclear disarmament.
But treating the principles as untouchable regardless of strategic change carries risks of its own, including a widening gap between declared policy and the deterrence architecture Japan’s allies are building around it.
For Japan, the choice is not simply whether to pursue nuclear armament or nuclear pacifism. The more immediate question is whether the third principle specifically – “not permitting the introduction” of nuclear weapons – can remain unchanged while Japan simultaneously asks the United States to strengthen extended nuclear deterrence.
The year-end revision of Japan’s security documents offers an opportunity to address that contradiction openly. Takaichi’s government must explain whether changing the third principle would materially strengthen deterrence – and whether any security benefits would outweigh the political and diplomatic costs.

articles.title: Assessing KMT Leader Cheng Li-Wun’s Political Narrative
articles.full_text:
KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun poses for a photo in front of the flags of the United States and the Republic of China during a visit to the Massachusetts Governor’s Office, June 5, 2026.
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Wayne Tan – professor at the Graduate Institute of International Politics, National Chung Hsing University (Taiwan), where he also serves as director of the Center for Indo-Pacific Strategy and Non-Traditional Security – is the 521st in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”  
How would you characterize Kuomintang (KMT) party chair Cheng Li-wun’s political narrative regarding Taiwan’s autonomy and sovereignty?
Political narratives should not be confused with strategic reality. One of the central arguments in my recent work is that Taiwan’s room for strategic maneuver is increasingly constrained by structural forces beyond the control of any Taiwanese political leaders. Whether one belongs to the KMT or the DPP [Democratic Progressive Party], Taiwan operates within an international system shaped by the intensifying strategic competition between the United States and China.
Viewed from this perspective, Cheng Li-wun’s narrative can be understood as a paradoxical attempt to maximize Taiwan’s autonomy through “self-restraint” rather than “strategic proactivity.” Unlike narratives that seek to reinforce sovereignty through greater international visibility, Cheng appears to argue that Taiwan’s de facto autonomy is best preserved by lowering the probability of military conflict and maintaining channels of communication with Beijing. 
However, it is important to realize that any genuine risk of military conflict across the Taiwan Strait arises not from Taiwan’s conduct, but from Beijing’s persistent use of gray-zone coercion, which has steadily eroded the stability of the status quo. Taiwan has never been the problem. Rather, it is the current Xi Jinping administration that has repeatedly generated instability through increasingly coercive actions in the region.
For this reason, I would be cautious about attributing excessive importance to Cheng’s political narrative. Taiwan’s leaders possess agency, but it is constrained agency. They can influence tactics, manage crises, and shape domestic political debate. What they cannot do is fundamentally alter the structural forces driving U.S.-China rivalry. As long as China continues to rise and the United States remains committed to preventing the emergence of a regional hegemon in Asia, Taiwan will remain one of the principal arenas of great-power competition. That reality is largely independent of which political party governs Taiwan or how its leaders frame questions of autonomy and sovereignty.
What are the strengths and weaknesses of Cheng’s rhetorical platform?
The strength of Cheng’s rhetoric is that it recognizes an uncomfortable reality often overlooked in Taiwan’s domestic political debate: military conflict would be catastrophic regardless of who prevails politically. In this sense, her discourse appeals to prudence rather than ideology. From an international relations perspective, reducing misperception and preserving diplomatic communication are entirely rational objectives. Thomas Schelling demonstrated decades ago that deterrence and communication are complementary rather than contradictory. Stability depends not only upon military capability but also upon credible signaling.
However, recognizing the reality mentioned above is not the same as overcoming it. The central weakness of Cheng’s platform lies in the implicit assumption that greater self-restraint or expanded dialogue can substantially reduce China’s ambitions toward Taiwan. That assumption is difficult to sustain when viewed through the logic of realism. If Beijing regards Taiwan as indispensable to its long-term regime security, legitimacy, and regional dominance, then changes in Taiwan’s rhetoric are unlikely to alter decision-makers’ fundamental objectives in Beijing.
This is the critical distinction between tactical tension reduction and strategic conflict resolution. Diplomatic engagement may lower the probability of accidental escalation in the short run, but it does not eliminate the underlying security competition. The continued existence of the Republic of China (Taiwan) represents an enduring legitimacy challenge for the government of PRC. As long as two competing political authorities each claim to represent a state legally, Beijing cannot fully consolidate its political legitimacy. This zero-sum rivalry has shaped the strategic calculations of every Chinese Communist Party leader since 1949 and helps explain why the Taiwan issue has remained central to PRC’s grand strategy. 
Compare and contrast the notion of Taiwan’s national identity between the KMT and the DPP.
To be sure, the two parties articulate different political narratives. The DPP increasingly defines Taiwan as a distinct democratic country whose legitimacy derives exclusively from the will of the Taiwanese people. The KMT, by contrast, continues to place greater emphasis on the constitutional framework of the ROC and generally advocates maintaining channels of communication with Beijing as a means of preserving stability. 
These differences matter for domestic elections and political discourse. But from the standpoint of international politics, they are of secondary importance. Neither party can alter the structural realities that dominate Taiwan’s security. Beijing has made clear that preventing Taiwan’s permanent separation is a core political interest. The United States, meanwhile, views Taiwan as a critical component of its strategy to prevent Beijing from being regional hegemony. Those are the forces that matter. Taiwan’s geographic location, the military balance across the Strait, and the intensity of Sino-American competition define the boundaries within which any Taiwanese government must operate.
Who are the principal audiences of Cheng’s political messaging?
Domestically, Cheng’s message primarily addresses voters who prioritize peace, economic stability, and risk reduction over ideological confrontation. These voters tend to evaluate cross-strait relations through practical rather than symbolic considerations.
A second audience consists of Taiwan’s business community, particularly firms deeply integrated into regional production networks. For these actors, geopolitical uncertainty translates directly into economic costs.
Internationally, Cheng’s messaging also speaks to observers in Washington, Beijing, Tokyo, and Southeast Asia by signaling that Taiwan’s democratic system contains multiple perspectives rather than a single unified position.
How do Beijing, Washington, and Tokyo view Cheng’s agenda?
Beijing, Washington, and Tokyo will judge Cheng not by her rhetoric but by whether her policies advance or hinder their strategic interests. Beijing may welcome dialogue, yet it will not abandon its objective of bringing Taiwan under control. Washington will support any Taiwanese leader who strengthens deterrence and resists Xi’s regime domination, regardless of party affiliation. Tokyo views Taiwan through the logic of balance of power: Beijing’s takeover would fundamentally undermine Japan’s security. 
The crucial point is that Taiwan’s domestic politics cannot override geopolitical realities. In an anarchic international system, small states possess agency, but only within limits imposed by great-power competition. Taiwan’s future therefore will be shaped primarily by the evolving balance of power between Washington and Beijing, not by the preferences or personalities of Taiwanese politicians.

articles.title: Should India Worry About the Mecca Pact?
articles.full_text:
The agreement is not directed against India, but it alters the strategic environment in which India-Pakistan relations play out.
(From left) Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif holding copies of the Mecca Pact after they signed the joint defense agreement in Mecca, August 7, 2026.
On August 7, the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, committing themselves to consider an attack on one as an attack on all. The Turkish Foreign Minister has indicated that the alliance could expand. This stands out as one of the most consequential shifts in the region’s ever-shifting power dynamics. That promise may well reshape the security dynamics of the entire region.
For New Delhi, the emergence of this framework warrants scrutiny. The agreement is not directed against India, but it alters the strategic environment in which India-Pakistan relations play out. Its implications for India, however, cannot be understood without first looking into why Pakistan sought such an arrangement.
Before May 2025, Pakistan’s concept of deterrence was not premised on fighting a prolonged war of attrition or achieving conventional military dominance. It was designed primarily to deny India escalation dominance in limited theaters while relying on nuclear deterrence to prevent a broader war.
The May 2025 conflict called that assumption into question. The conflict rapidly climbed up several rungs of the escalation ladder and spread geographically beyond what many observers had anticipated. The conflict demonstrated that nuclear deterrence does not necessarily rule out sustained conventional fighting below the nuclear threshold.
For Pakistan, this brings about a significant strategic dilemma. Islamabad cannot afford to go through recurrent military crises that pile on prolonged economic costs. The lesson of May 2025, therefore, is not simply that Pakistan must step up its ability to fight. It is that Pakistan must raise the potential costs of future confrontation sufficiently high that India cannot count on achieving decisive conventional superiority without triggering broader strategic consequences.
The Mecca framework feeds into this objective directly. A NATO Article 5-style commitment involving Saudi Arabia and Türkiye opens up the possibility that an attack on Pakistan could trigger diplomatic, economic, and military consequences beyond the immediate South Asian theater.
Pakistan’s motivations extend beyond deterrence. In the past, Islamabad has run up against the risks associated with excessive dependence on a single source of military supplies. The United States cut off military supplies to Pakistan during the 1965 India-Pakistan war. Today, approximately 80 percent of Pakistan’s weapons systems are Chinese-made. Such dependence can cut into autonomy by leaving military preparedness vulnerable to the political calculations and supply-chain priorities of an external power.
Access to alternative suppliers and production networks could make it easier to sustain military operations while paring down the risks associated with putting all eggs in one basket. Diversifying defense partnerships can, therefore, give Pakistan greater strategic leeway.
The framework also points to a broader recognition that military dependence ultimately ties down strategic freedom. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan all have incentives to build up indigenous defense production rather than remain stuck with great powers whose interests may veer away from their own.
Their capabilities are complementary. Saudi Arabia can potentially provide financial resources for large-scale investment, Türkiye brings a relatively advanced indigenous defense industry, while Pakistan chips in with operational experience and an established defense-industrial base. Joint research, technology sharing, and co-production could, therefore, yield capabilities that would be difficult for any one of the three to develop independently.
The framework must also be understood in the context of broader transformation of Pakistan’s relations with West Asia. Over the past decade, India has substantially built up its economic and diplomatic engagement with the Gulf. New Delhi’s growing economic weight has allowed it to develop relationships with West Asian states that reach beyond traditional political ties.
From Pakistan’s perspective, this has gradually narrowed down some of the strategic space it once held in the region. Pakistan cannot realistically compete with India on an economic scale. Its response has, therefore, centered on areas where it holds greater comparative value, particularly defense cooperation. Pakistan can gain greater relevance by offering capabilities that Gulf states increasingly view as valuable to their security architecture. The emerging framework hands over to Islamabad an institutional mechanism through which it can translate its defense capabilities into broader diplomatic influence in West Asia.
Pakistan’s approach to the region is also not zero-sum. Islamabad has shown an ability to keep up relations with Iran even as Tehran’s relations with several Gulf states have deteriorated. This balancing act can itself become a source of leverage. Iran has an interest in keeping channels open with Pakistan, particularly when Islamabad can help advance negotiations with the United States or contribute to post-war reconciliation with Gulf states.
This opens up another potential arena of competition with India. Iran had, to some extent, become an important partner for New Delhi over the previous decade. Pakistan’s emerging strategy is to cut down India’s relative influence by maintaining credible relations with Iran. Its success will depend on Islamabad’s ability to hedge between competing regional blocs without letting either side write it off as an outright adversary.
For India, the geographic and political boundaries of a future India-Pakistan confrontation may be less predictable. A conflict that was previously restricted to South Asia could call forth stronger political and diplomatic reactions from West Asian states.
In an active theater of conflict, the framework may matter more. India appeared to be taken aback by the extent of support China poured into Pakistan during the May conflict. Future crises could bring in additional external support from Türkiye and Saudi Arabia. Even if these states stay out of direct combat, intelligence sharing, technological assistance, logistics, and military supplies could disrupt India’s calculations.
Nevertheless, India should avoid interpreting the Mecca framework as an anti-Indian alliance. Its logic is based on deterrence for states that believe they need greater collective security to prevent war. Treating the arrangement as inherently hostile could turn into a self-fulfilling prophecy.
If India responds by actively balancing against the Mecca framework, it could encourage the latter’s members to view India as a common strategic threat, giving the alliance an orientation it does not necessarily hold today. Such a response would risk multiplying India’s strategic challenges, narrowing down its own room for maneuver in West Asia.
Paradoxically, the framework could also bring about incentives for restraint for both Pakistan and India. The framework’s deterrent value will hinge on the credibility of its collective-defense commitment, and that credibility gives all three members a stake in preventing the agreement from being tested unnecessarily. Pakistan, therefore, has an incentive to hold back from actions that could force its partners into a confrontation they may not otherwise seek.
India would also have reason to factor in this credibility problem. If New Delhi writes off the agreement as merely declaratory, it runs up against the risk of miscalculation. The uncertainty surrounding third-party involvement could lead India to exercise greater caution during a crisis.
India and Pakistan are already bearing substantial economic costs from entrenched rivalry, but the consequences of a wider regional confrontation would cut into the economic interests of countries in West Asia. The resulting economic disruption would weigh on both India and Pakistan.
As South Asia becomes more closely linked with the security architecture of West Asia, sustained dialogue between Pakistan and India has become a strategic necessity.

articles.title: Is Badakhshan Becoming the Epicenter of Anti-Taliban Resistance?
articles.full_text:
Mounting resistance and ethnic tension are testing Taliban rule in Afghanistan’s north.
On August 9, Taliban officials claimed to have captured 74 light and heavy weapons that were allegedly being smuggled in from Pakistan to support what they termed “subversive and destabilizing activities.” Islamabad strongly denied the claim as baseless and urged Kabul not to let Afghan soil be used against Pakistan. 
The Taliban’s claim insinuated that Pakistan was supporting the resistance movement that has been brewing for some time in northern Afghanistan but has escalated to alarming levels since July. The movement is especially strong in the strategically important northeastern Badakhshan province, which borders not only Pakistan but also China and Tajikistan. 
Groups like the Ahmad Massoud-led National Resistance Front (NRF) and the Yasin Zia-led Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF) announced resistance to the Taliban soon after their return to power in August 2021. But the resistance has remained limited and inconsequential until the more recently established Qayyum Malang-led Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, or the Homeland Guards, launched a far more aggressive campaign against the Taliban in Badakhshan last month. In mid-July, the Sipahiyan-i-Mihan even briefly captured Yaftal-e-Paeen district in the province. A few weeks later, the AFF claimed to have killed four members of the Taliban in two separate attacks in Jalalabad and Nuristan provinces. It has also been reported that Taliban personnel leave their posts at night in certain parts of Takhar province because of increasing attacks.
As trouble brews for the Taliban in Badakhshan and some neighboring provinces, ethnic Tajik groups like the Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, NRF, and AFF are not the only challenge the Taliban is facing in the region. The Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), which has launched several high-profile attacks against the Taliban since the latter’s return to power, is also an ongoing source of concern. A couple of weeks after the district headquarters in Yaftal briefly fell to the Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, ISKP assassinated Badakhshan’s well-connected Taliban director for information and culture, Zabihullah Amiri, in the province.
The Taliban have responded to the challenge with increasing restrictions on movement in the province and by sending in largely Pashtun reinforcements to the Tajik-majority province. The Taliban are also having to rely on hardline but recalcitrant local powerbrokers within their ranks like Juma Khan Fateh. A former small-time shopkeeper from the Shakhdara village in Nusay district, he rose through the ranks of the Taliban since 2013 to become one of the most powerful figures in Badakhshan, and yet Fateh has remained an enigma for the Taliban leadership. 
Reported to have stated that he has around 10,000 armed men under his command, Fateh has been consolidating his power in Badakhshan through gold mining revenues since becoming administrator of his home district upon the return of the Taliban to power in Afghanistan. He is even reported to have continued gold mining operations in Badakhshan in defiance of the Taliban’s ban on such operations. Nevertheless, he was flown back to Badakhshan in August amid growing attacks by opposition groups, demonstrating the Taliban’s desperation for support against resistance to its rule.

articles.title: Japan’s Nuclear Taboo Is Starting to Crack
articles.full_text:
Whether or not Japan’s nuclear policy is actually revised, the very fact that such a revision is being openly debated is a striking development.
August has been a solemn month in Japan for more than 80 years. Although Japan formally signed the Instrument of Surrender on September 2, 1945, the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on August 6 and 9, respectively, and Emperor Hirohito’s radio announcement on August 15 accepting the terms of surrender have made August a month from which the Japanese psyche cannot escape. Every year since the Pacific War ended in Japan’s defeat, during August the nation has mourned its war dead and reflected on the horrors of a conflict that inflicted immense suffering and destruction upon the country. The resolve that Japan must never again endure such an ordeal lingers in the air of the sweltering Japanese summer.
But this year, another issue besides the memory of war has been generating heated debate in the Japanese media: will the Takaichi administration revise the government’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles in the upcoming revision of Japan’s national security documents? 
Japanese media outlets have been closely scrutinizing Takaichi’s remarks on Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles, under which Japan pledges not to possess, produce, or allow the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. This attention stems from Takaichi’s previous position that at least the principle concerning the non-introduction of nuclear weapons should be reconsidered in the interests of Japan’s national security. In an edited volume she published in 2024, Takaichi even argued that Japan’s current nuclear policy was not “realistic” when it came to ensuring the credibility of the U.S. extended nuclear deterrent.
The fact that she has not categorically ruled out revising the principles since becoming prime minister has fueled speculation that she could embark on a major shift in Japan’s decades-old nuclear policy – essentially distancing the country from its longstanding commitment to refrain from assuming any role in the deployment of nuclear weapons, even for defensive purposes. 
Questioned about her current stance on Japan’s nuclear policy, Takaichi has maintained that her government “remains committed to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles as a matter of policy.” At the same time, she has declined to “say definitively what their final wording will look like” in the revised security documents. In other words, Takaichi has reiterated – even on the anniversaries of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki – that the existing nuclear policy remains in place for now, while leaving open the question of how nuclear weapons will be addressed in the future.
Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, Takaichi’s point man for drafting the new national security policies, has also hinted that a revision of Japan’s nuclear policy may be on the table. Appearing on a conservative online program, Koizumi acknowledged that nuclear weapons are “a difficult issue for Japan to discuss,” but argued that it is one that cannot be avoided. 
He went further, saying that “we must recognize the sense of crisis we face and discuss and pursue every possible policy option without treating anything as taboo.” He also referred to the efforts of Finland and France to strengthen their nuclear deterrence. For Koizumi, preserving existing policies should not take priority over the fundamental responsibility of protecting Japan.
Whether or not Japan’s nuclear policy is actually revised in the immediate future, the very fact that such a revision is being openly debated is a striking development in Japanese policy discourse. For decades, any positive discussion of the role nuclear weapons might play in Japan’s security policy could be a career breaker for Japanese politicians. In 1999, Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Defense Nishimura Shingo was forced to resign after a Japanese magazine quoted him as saying that Japan should consider becoming a nuclear power. And although he did not meet the same fate as Nishimura, LDP policy chief Nakagawa Shoichi came under intense scrutiny in 2006 after suggesting that Japan should debate nuclear policy in depth.
Even discussing the memory and legacy of nuclear weapons has been a tightrope for Japanese politicians. In 2007, then-Defense Minister Kyuma Fumio came under fierce criticism after saying that, although “countless people suffered terribly,” he viewed the atomic bombings as having brought the war to an end and that he had “no intention of holding a grudge against the United States over it.” He resigned less than two weeks after making the remarks. 
However, based on the remarks by Takaichi and Koizumi, which appear to have generated little public backlash, statements about putting nuclear weapons on the table no longer seem to be regarded as political gaffes. 
Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles are among the few remaining national security taboos for a country that was once deeply committed to pacifism. Since entering the 21st century, Japan has crossed one security taboo after another: deploying the Self-Defense Forces to active conflict zones, legitimizing the exercise of the right of collective self-defense, establishing a National Security Council and centralized intelligence capabilities, opening a military base overseas, and greenlighting the export of lethal weapons. All of these would have been difficult to imagine in the previous century; today, they are established facts of Japanese security policy.
While Takaichi has not altered the Three Non-Nuclear Principles – yet – she has indicated that she would follow a precedent set by the Democratic Party of Japan government. In 2010, then-Foreign Minister Okada Katsuya stated that, in an extreme emergency threatening Japan’s national security, “the government of the day must make the decision with the nation’s fate at stake and explain its decision to the public.” This interpretation effectively creates a potential exception to the principle prohibiting the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japan, without formally abandoning the Three Non-Nuclear Principles themselves.
However, even if an existing exception has effectively rendered one of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles moot in practice, formally revising it would carry enormous symbolic significance. If the Takaichi administration embarks on an official revision of Japan’s nuclear policy, it would mark yet another postwar taboo overturned. Such a move would have been astonishing in 20th century Japan, but it would also fit the broader trajectory of Japan’s increasingly assertive security policy.
